November 17, 2026
Abstract

Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant pp-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent’s relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent’s actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

Keywords: coding agents, large language models, selective inference, post-selection inference, hypothesis testing, specification search, replication

JEL Codes: C12, C18, C45, C52, C63

1 Introduction

Coding agents, large language model (LLM)-based systems that can interact with a computing environment by reading files, writing and executing code, and invoking command-line tools, first emerged around 2023 (Lucas and Open Interpreter Contributors, 2023) before gaining widespread use in early 2025 (Anthropic, 2025) with the introduction of Claude Code. Since then, “agentic” AI has rapidly gained a foothold in the market, with estimated annualized spending on AI coding applications reaching $34 billion by September 2026, up from approximately $4.4 billion in 2025 (Menlo Ventures, 2026). While their initial user base was mostly concentrated among software engineers and so-called “vibe coders”, programmers who delegate all their coding to AI agents, their applicability to tasks ranging from data analysis and scientific simulations to literature reviews and paper editing has contributed to their growing adoption in empirical science.

Indeed, empirical researchers are increasingly delegating large parts of data analysis and scientific modeling to coding agents (Codreanu et al., 2026; Hermle et al., 2026; Johnston et al., 2026). In a survey of social scientists in Feb–Mar 2026, Lyttelton et al. (2026) found that 20% of quantitative social scientists, including 39% of economists, regularly used coding agents. A researcher typically provides a coding agent with data and a description of the question they want to test or the design they want to implement. Like a human analyst, the agent can then inspect the data, choose variables, estimate a few models, and inspect their results before deciding what implementation is worth reporting. While this recent development has the potential to drastically speed up empirical science, it also poses a threat to valid statistical inference. Unless the precise hypothesis and method to test it are fully specified in a type of agentic pre-registration design, the fact that coding agents typically pull a rich information set into their context window before formulating their hypothesis means that classic statistical inferential guarantees, which assume the hypothesis is specified before looking at the data, will typically fail to hold.

The adoption of coding agents leads to a new “agentic” form of selective inference with several unique traits. Like human researchers, coding agents can search over a tremendously vast space of models. Unlike humans, however, coding agents are programs that can be controlled and replayed on counterfactual versions of the data. Moreover, the final output of a coding agent’s workflow is a piece of executable code. In this paper, we exploit this unique combination of replayability of the open-ended, black-box selection process and executability of the selected analysis to restore valid inference.

We develop a method that detects when a coding agent chooses its analysis based on the results it sees and corrects the reported pp-value for such data-driven selection. In particular, because coding agents are programs, we can reset and replay them on resampled versions of the data. This offers a way around the black-box nature of agent-driven selection by empirically estimating how often agents reselect a given analysis when it looks statistically favorable on a dataset. We can estimate this frequency by exploiting the fact that coding agents emit executable analysis code. After an agent has selected and coded up its analysis, our replay method executes that code on subsamples of the data, sorting these subsamples by how favorable their pp-values look compared to the agent’s original pp-value. If the agent is more likely to reselect its analysis on favorable subsamples, this offers evidence of data-driven selection by the agent. The ratio of the frequency with which the agent selects the analysis on favorable subsamples to its overall selection frequency, which we refer to as the selection multiplier λ\lambda, measures how strongly the agent’s selection depends on the results. The idea is visualized in Figure 1: the coding agent, by selecting an analysis q∗q^{*} from the space of potential analyses, distorts the uniformity characteristic of a calibrated pp-value, leading to the pp-values reported by the agent piling up near zero. Our method estimates this distortion by replaying the agent and corrects for it, restoring the uniformity and hence validity of the corrected pp-values.

We show that λ\lambda is all that is needed to 1) detect whether a given result was selected and 2) correct the agent’s pp-value and restore its statistical guarantees, building on Sood (2024). More precisely, we establish that the resulting corrected pp-value is asymptotically valid conditional on the agent’s selection, that it loses no first-order power relative to the oracle correction where the agent’s selection probabilities are known exactly, and that it inherits the consistency of the original test it corrects. We also show how to construct valid confidence bands for the corrected pp-value, and provide conditions under which these results hold uniformly over a class of null distributions.

Our simulations and applications demonstrate the value of both detecting and correcting for coding agents’ selection. When asked for “one compelling, defensible finding”, the latest frontier coding agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol (at high effort), report a significant (p≤0.05p\leq 0.05) result 54 and 88% of the time, respectively, on simulated datasets where all true effects are zero. When given data from a seminal economics paper (Card and Krueger, 1994) and asked to find the most statistically compelling result, GPT-6.1-Sol is nearly 2 times more likely to report its chosen analysis when it looks statistically favorable, while Claude Sonnet 5.5 consistently commits to the same specification. In another application, to a replication analysis of data relating to immigration and welfare support (Brady and Finnigan, 2014; Breznau et al., 2022; Borjas and Breznau, 2026), GPT-6-Luna explicitly attempts to restrain its own search, yet it reselects its analysis 2.42 times as often when the analysis is significant. Across different settings and AI models, the agents exhibit inconsistent behavior: sometimes they strongly select results, while claiming they do not; sometimes they do not select.

The agents also attempt to self-correct, applying multiplicity corrections to their reported results. We argue and show empirically that these attempts do not restore coverage for a given analysis, as the family of analyses they correct for is itself data-dependent. These findings highlight a major benefit of our proposed method: it does not rely on any model of how exactly coding agents behave and select analyses. Instead, it explicitly estimates the agents’ selective behavior and uses this estimate to correct for the distortions it induces.

Formally, we treat the agents’ selection rule as an arbitrary black-box selection mapping from the data to the reported results. The only assumption our method requires on the agents is that their selection behavior stabilizes asymptotically, and that they are able to accurately report on the analyses they implement. Our method therefore applies to essentially any coding agent, regardless of the model family or generation. This is crucial because AI agents are a moving target, with specific findings about their behavior being short-lived (Queen and Zou, 2026).

The proposed method also places no restrictions on the kinds of estimators and inference procedures the agents can implement, other than that their pp-values are asymptotically exact. This is important because part of coding agents’ appeal is that they can explore an analysis space as broad as humans can, holding the promise to accelerate empirical research. More broadly, our goal in developing this method was to intervene minimally on researchers’ preferred agentic workflow, allowing researchers to simply layer it on top. Our method achieves this by estimating and correcting for any selective behavior after the analysis is complete, at the cost of repeated agent runs.

Related literature.

Our paper contributes to the literature on inference after data-dependent analysis, including sample splitting (Cox, 1975), simultaneous post-selection inference (Berk et al., 2013), conditional selective inference (Fithian et al., 2014; Tibshirani et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; Tian and Taylor, 2018; Andrews et al., 2024), and adaptive data analysis based on algorithmic stability (Dwork et al., 2015; Zrnic and Jordan, 2023); see Kuchibhotla et al. (2022); Neufeld et al. (2026) for useful reviews. We build most directly on two recent sub-strands of the literature dealing with black-box conditional selective inference (Markovic et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Liu and Panigrahi, 2025) and pp-value-based selective inference (Sood, 2024). Our contribution to this literature is to develop a computationally simple method to restore the validity of selected pp-values that imposes minimal assumptions on the black-box selection rule and the data-generating process; see Section 2.3 for a detailed comparison. The paper also connects work on specification search and researcher discretion (White, 2000; Simmons et al., 2011; McCloskey and Michaillat, 2026) with the growing literature on coding agents in empirical research (Korinek, 2025). Recent studies empirically examine agents’ analytical choices (Bertran et al., 2026; Gao and Xiao, 2026; McCully, 2026; Galiani et al., 2026; Asher et al., 2026), their sensitivity to prompting (Asher et al., 2026; Miao et al., 2026), and their influence on human researchers’ analytical decisions (Herdağdelen et al., 2026), extending similar evidence of variation across human analysts (Silberzahn et al., 2018; Huntington-Klein et al., 2021; Breznau et al., 2022), though other research has cast doubt on the durability of empirical findings about LLMs (Queen and Zou, 2026). Within this literature, Miao et al. (2026) propose an agentic bootstrap that evaluates agents’ findings relative to the distribution of alternative findings they generate when their prompts are perturbed, while Fishman and Sekeres (2026) study how the cheap specification search that coding agents enable changes editorial screening. We complement these contributions by developing a method for both detecting and correcting any distortions to classical statistical guarantees induced by coding-agent-driven empirical research. Moreover, because our correction is learned from the agent’s actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, it does not require us to assume, understand, or anticipate its analytical behavior. This provides a durable framework for valid statistical inference even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly.

2 Inference after coding agents

2.1 Setup

Coding agents.

We start by describing and formalizing, at a high level, how empirical research with coding agents takes place. We refer the readers to Appendix C.1 for useful background on how coding agents function. Consider the following empirical workflow. A researcher wants to investigate the effect of the minimum wage on employment using one or several datasets. They place those datasets in a folder on their computer and launch their coding agent of choice. Then they tell the coding agent their research question, point it to the data files, and outline the design that they want it to execute. The instructions for the coding agent can vary considerably in how precisely they describe the setting and the estimand the researcher wants to estimate. For example, the researcher could specify that they want the coding agent to estimate a staggered difference-in-differences design or a synthetic controls estimator, and provide additional files specifying the exact data structure and experimental design. Alternatively, the researcher might simply ask the coding agent to “find me something interesting”. The coding agent then goes to work, inspects the data, writes code, executes preliminary analyses, revises its estimates, and finally settles on an estimate it reports back to the researcher.

To formalize this workflow, let R=rR=r denote the researcher’s initial prompt, interpreted broadly to include the instructions and additional context available to the agent, including codebooks, project instructions, and descriptions of the research design. Let DD denote the data supplied to the agent, viewed as a random object that can comprise several files in different formats (e.g. .csv, .dta, .xlsx).

Importantly, throughout the paper, we treat the initial prompt and context rr as fixed and chosen independently of the data DD. This rules out data-dependent revisions of the prompt by the human researcher, including feedback based on intermediate results. Such data-dependent revisions add another layer of human selection on top of the coding agent’s own selection. This paper focuses on machine-driven selective inference, that is, selection carried out by coding agents that, unlike the human researcher’s selection, can be replayed. Adding human decisions into the workflow would connect this setting to the well-established literature on pp-hacking, which is not the focus of this article.

Formal setup.

We use 𝒬\mathcal{Q} to denote a collection of possible analyses produced by the agent. Following Fithian et al. (2014), we think of a given q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q} as specifying a model ℳ\mathcal{M} and a corresponding null hypothesis H0⊂ℳH_{0}\subset\mathcal{M},

q=(ℳ,H0)∈𝒬,q=(\mathcal{M},H_{0})\in\mathcal{Q},

and the alternative hypothesis is ℳ∖H0\mathcal{M}\setminus H_{0}. For each q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}, we write ℳq\mathcal{M}_{q} and H0,qH_{0,q} for its model and null hypothesis, respectively. Then, the coding agent, after being given the initial prompt rr and the dataset DD, can be modeled as a stochastic selection mapping,

Q=𝒜r​(D,Ξ),Q=\mathcal{A}_{r}(D,\Xi), (1)

where Ξ\Xi captures randomness in the LLM’s response and possibly in the outputs of its tool uses (e.g., when it executes a command whose output depends on a random seed). We hold the precise language model, tools, and runtime configurations used for the coding agent fixed as part of 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r}. The null hypothesis H0,qH_{0,q} and statistical model ℳq\mathcal{M}_{q} reflect any decisions the agent makes about sample restrictions, data filtering, outcome construction, etc., as those change the sampling population and specific outcome the null hypothesis is constructed around. Given this selection mapping, whenever we write Pr⁡(Q=q)\Pr(Q=q) below, this is shorthand for Pr⁡(𝒜r​(D,Ξ)=q)\Pr(\mathcal{A}_{r}(D,\Xi)=q). We assume that Ξ\Xi is independent of DD and that 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} is jointly measurable so that Pr⁡(Q=q∣D=d)=Pr⁡(𝒜r​(d,Ξ)=q)\Pr(Q=q\mid D=d)=\Pr(\mathcal{A}_{r}(d,\Xi)=q), the probability that the agent selects qq on a given dataset dd, is defined for every dd.

We assume that the agent also emits code to implement an inferential procedure that tests the null, using a p-value pq​(D)p_{q}(D). In line with classical conditional selective inference, we assume each analysis qq has a fixed, valid p-value, that is, q↦pq​(D)q\mapsto p_{q}(D). That is, the agent can select qq adaptively based on the data, but given qq, it does not “p-hack” further by choosing among alternative p-value procedures based on the data. Note that this does account for a broader definition of p-hacking where the agent commits to a different model or null q′q^{\prime} based on the corresponding p-value pq′p_{q^{\prime}}. Moreover, this assumption can be relaxed to allow for inferential selection as well, but we leave that for later work.

Example 1 (Motivating example: choosing a population).

Let us return to the minimum-wage example. Suppose the researcher provides an initial prompt asking the agent to investigate the employment effects of a minimum wage increase. For illustration, suppose the agent considers two candidate populations: teenagers and adults. Each population gg defines an analysis qgq_{g} consisting of a model ℳg\mathcal{M}_{g} and a null hypothesis H0,gH_{0,g} of no average employment effect, qg=(ℳg,H0,g)q_{g}=(\mathcal{M}_{g},H_{0,g}). For each qgq_{g}, the agent emits a test whose p-value pg​(D)p_{g}(D) would be valid if qgq_{g} were pre-specified.

The agent will generally look at the data before deciding which analysis to report. For example, it could choose to focus on teenagers if their estimated employment response is larger than the effect for adults. Even if the agent accurately describes the selected analysis and correctly implements the prescribed procedure, the reported pp-value will generally not be valid conditional on the agent’s selection. This is because the agent uses the same data to select qgq_{g} and test H0,gH_{0,g}.

Correcting for this selection requires answering the following question: “How likely was the agent to select this analysis on this particular dataset?” In practice, we propose to estimate this answer by rerunning the agent with the exact same prompt but a new version of the dataset. Does the agent still focus on teenagers when this new dataset shows smaller effects for them? For this, we only need to be able to replay the agent and observe its selection, with no requirement to know or intervene on its analytical behavior, in particular the steps it takes to arrive at its final reported analysis.

Selective inference.

Example 1 illustrates the distinction between validity for a fixed analysis and validity conditional on the agent selecting that analysis. Even if pq​(D)p_{q}(D) is valid for a prespecified analysis q=(ℳq,H0,q)q=(\mathcal{M}_{q},H_{0,q}), pq​(D)p_{q}(D) need not be valid if the agent selects analysis qq after inspecting the data DD.

To see how the selective inference problem arises more formally, first consider a pre-specified analysis q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q} that does not depend on the data. Let 𝒫0,q\mathcal{P}_{0,q} denote the class of data-generating laws under which the fixed null hypothesis H0,qH_{0,q} holds. Then, classical statistical validity requires,

PrP⁡(pq​(D)≤α)≤α,P∈𝒫0,q,α∈(0,1),\Pr_{P}\!\left(p_{q}(D)\leq\alpha\right)\leq\alpha,\qquad P\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q},\quad\alpha\in(0,1), (2)

that is, the p-value is valid for any given significance level α\alpha, for repeated samples from PP. Now, assume the coding agent selected analysis qq after looking at the data. Then the guarantee

PrP⁡(pq​(D)≤α∣Q=q)≤α\Pr_{P}\!\left(p_{q}(D)\leq\alpha\mid Q=q\right)\leq\alpha

need not hold, because the distribution of pq​(D)p_{q}(D) conditional on Q=qQ=q will in general not coincide with the fixed-analysis distribution above. For a visual representation of the difference between the two distributions, see Figure 1. Note that this does not require the coding agent to search for favorable results deliberately. Simply inspecting the data, trying alternative specifications, or revising an analysis after inspecting the results makes the selected analysis QQ depend on the same data used to compute the p-value.

Fully pre-specifying the analysis in the researcher’s initial prompt would avoid this source of selection, but would also limit the flexibility that makes coding agents useful as empirical analysts and does not reflect their typical use (Hitzig et al., 2026; Codreanu et al., 2026, see e.g.). We therefore allow the researcher’s initial prompt rr to constrain the agent’s analysis to varying degrees, ranging from complete preregistration to a generic open-ended prompt (“find me something interesting”). One could also potentially resolve the selection problem through data splitting, but this would similarly restrict the agent’s flexibility. See Fithian et al. (2014) for a more detailed comparison between conditional selective inference and data splitting.

Our objective is to restore the validity of the p-value conditional on the selected analysis, following the conditional selective inference literature (Fithian et al., 2014; Tibshirani et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016). Specifically, for any selected analysis qq with PrP⁡(Q=q)>0\Pr_{P}\!\left(Q=q\right)>0, we aim to construct a p-value pqselp_{q}^{\mathrm{sel}} satisfying

PrP⁡(pqsel≤α∣Q=q)≤α,P∈𝒫0,q,α∈(0,1).\Pr_{P}\!\left(p_{q}^{\mathrm{sel}}\leq\alpha\mid Q=q\right)\leq\alpha,\qquad P\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q},\quad\alpha\in(0,1).

In doing so, we aim to provide valid inferences while minimally intervening in researchers’ empirical workflow, allowing them to exploit the versatility of coding agents as empirical analysts.

Example 2 (Technical example: stochastic selection).

Consider two distinct analyses q1q_{1} and q2q_{2}, each with its own fixed p-value procedure. Suppose that, given the data, the agent selects q1q_{1} with probability 1−pq1​(D)1-p_{q_{1}}(D) and otherwise selects q2q_{2}, so that more favorable evidence for q1q_{1} makes its selection more likely.

Fix P∈𝒫0,q1P\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q_{1}} and suppose that pq1​(D)p_{q_{1}}(D) is exactly calibrated, so that U1=pq1​(D)U_{1}=p_{q_{1}}(D) is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1].

Then, the probability of selecting q1q_{1} is

PrP⁡(Q=q1)=∫01(1−t)​𝑑t=12\Pr_{P}(Q=q_{1})=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\,dt=\frac{1}{2}

and the cdf of U1U_{1} conditional on selection is

PrP⁡(U1≤u∣Q=q1)=∫0u(1−t)​𝑑t1/2=2​u−u2.\Pr_{P}(U_{1}\leq u\mid Q=q_{1})=\frac{\int_{0}^{u}(1-t)\,dt}{1/2}=2u-u^{2}.

A nominal 5%5\% test therefore rejects with probability 0.09750.0975 conditional on Q=q1Q=q_{1}, even though its fixed-analysis p-value is exactly calibrated.

The transformed p-value,

pq1sel=2​pq1​(D)−pq1​(D)2,p_{q_{1}}^{\mathrm{sel}}=2p_{q_{1}}(D)-p_{q_{1}}(D)^{2},

however, is uniformly distributed conditional on Q=q1Q=q_{1}, and restores exact selective validity.

Correcting the p-value.

In Example 2, the correction evaluates the conditional cdf of the selected p-value at its observed value. We now develop this construction for a general analysis qq. For this, fix a null law P∈𝒫0,qP\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q} under which PrP⁡(Q=q)>0\Pr_{P}(Q=q)>0. For ease of exposition, assume first that the fixed-analysis p-value is exactly uniform under the null, that is,

PrP⁡(pq​(D)≤u)=u,u∈[0,1].\Pr_{P}\!\left(p_{q}(D)\leq u\right)=u,\quad u\in[0,1].

Our theoretical results below replace this assumption with asymptotic exact calibration. We suppress the dependence on PP and rr in the objects defined below. Here and below, pq​(D)p_{q}(D) is the p-value obtained by applying the fixed procedure associated with qq to DD, whether or not the agent selects qq based on DD.

Define

Hq​(u):=PrP⁡(pq​(D)≤u∣Q=q)H_{q}(u):=\Pr_{P}\!\left(p_{q}(D)\leq u\mid Q=q\right)

as the conditional cdf of the fixed-analysis p-value among datasets on which the agent selects qq. If HqH_{q} were known, the canonical probability integral transform would give the oracle selection-corrected p-value

pqsel=Hq​(pq​(D)),p_{q}^{\mathrm{sel}}=H_{q}\!\left(p_{q}(D)\right),

which satisfies

pqsel|Q=q∼Unif⁡(0,1).p_{q}^{\mathrm{sel}}\mid Q=q\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1). (3)

By Bayes’ rule, this correction has the following intuitive interpretation:

Hq​(u)\displaystyle H_{q}(u) =PrP⁡(pq​(D)≤u)​PrP⁡(Q=q∣pq​(D)≤u)PrP⁡(Q=q)\displaystyle=\Pr_{P}\!\left(p_{q}(D)\leq u\right)\frac{\Pr_{P}\!\left(Q=q\mid p_{q}(D)\leq u\right)}{\Pr_{P}(Q=q)} (4)
=u​λq​(u),\displaystyle=u\,\lambda_{q}(u), (5)

where

λq​(u):=PrP⁡(Q=q∣pq​(D)≤u)PrP⁡(Q=q)\lambda_{q}(u):=\frac{\Pr_{P}\!\left(Q=q\mid p_{q}(D)\leq u\right)}{\Pr_{P}(Q=q)}

is the selection multiplier, that is, the relative probability of selecting analysis qq given that the p-value under that analysis is at least as favorable as uu. The second equality follows from the assumption that the fixed-analysis p-value is exactly valid under the null. Thus, λq​(u)\lambda_{q}(u) compares the probability of selecting qq among datasets where that same analysis produces a p-value at most uu with its overall selection probability under the same null law PP. Writing dd for the observed dataset, this gives,

pqsel=pq​(d)​λq​(pq​(d)).p_{q}^{\mathrm{sel}}=p_{q}(d)\,\lambda_{q}\!\left(p_{q}(d)\right).

That is, the selective p-value equals the p-value actually reported by the coding agent, pq​(d)p_{q}(d), adjusted by the relative probability of the agent selecting the same analysis on datasets that are at least as statistically favorable as dd (where the p-value is at least as small as the reported one). When λq​(u)>1\lambda_{q}(u)>1, analysis qq is more likely to be selected on datasets where its evidence is favorable, and a p-value equal to uu must be adjusted upward. Conversely, λq​(u)<1\lambda_{q}(u)<1 means that qq is less likely to be selected in this favorable tail, and the correction adjusts the p-value downward. If the event {Q=q}\{Q=q\} is independent of pq​(D)p_{q}(D) under PP, then λq​(u)=1\lambda_{q}(u)=1 for every u∈(0,1]u\in(0,1] and no correction is required. In the stochastic selection Example 2 above, PrP⁡(Q=q1∣U1≤u)=1−u/2\Pr_{P}(Q=q_{1}\mid U_{1}\leq u)=1-u/2, compared with PrP⁡(Q=q1)=1/2\Pr_{P}(Q=q_{1})=1/2, so that λq1​(u)=2−u\lambda_{q_{1}}(u)=2-u, recovering Hq1​(u)=u​λq1​(u)=2​u−u2H_{q_{1}}(u)=u\lambda_{q_{1}}(u)=2u-u^{2}.

For a single reported analysis, the multiplier depends on just two selection probabilities. Define

a1,q​(u):=PrP⁡(Q=q∣pq​(D)≤u),a0,q​(u):=PrP⁡(Q=q∣pq​(D)>u).a_{1,q}(u):=\Pr_{P}\!\left(Q=q\mid p_{q}(D)\leq u\right),\qquad a_{0,q}(u):=\Pr_{P}\!\left(Q=q\mid p_{q}(D)>u\right).

Since pq​(D)p_{q}(D) is uniform under the null,

PrP⁡(Q=q)=u​a1,q​(u)+(1−u)​a0,q​(u),\Pr_{P}(Q=q)=u\,a_{1,q}(u)+(1-u)\,a_{0,q}(u),

and therefore

Hq​(u)=u​a1,q​(u)u​a1,q​(u)+(1−u)​a0,q​(u).H_{q}(u)=\frac{u\,a_{1,q}(u)}{u\,a_{1,q}(u)+(1-u)\,a_{0,q}(u)}. (6)

Evaluating this expression at the p-value on the observed dataset dd, pq​(d)p_{q}(d), then gives the desired correction. Thus, to correct the reported p-value for selection, we only need to estimate two tractable objects: the probability of selecting analysis qq on alternative datasets with pp-values smaller and larger than pq​(d)p_{q}(d). Assuming we can sample such alternative datasets, which we will return to below, Hq​(u)H_{q}(u) can be estimated by simply replaying the agent on them.

We emphasize once more that the exact uniformity of the fixed-analysis pp-value was a simplifying assumption to ease exposition in this section. The theoretical results below require only asymptotic exact calibration (Assumption 3).

2.2 Estimator

2.2.1 Selective p-value

We estimate the selection correction by combining two operations on random subsamples of the original data: executing the agent’s emitted program and replaying the agent. Section 2.2.2 describes how we draw subsamples of size mm from the original data DnD_{n} of size n>mn>m. We will index a dataset DD by its sample size kk, e.g. DkD_{k}, where needed for clarity. The reported estimate and fixed-analysis p-value continue to use the full dataset. We use the subsampled datasets to estimate the selection multiplier at sample size mm. The selection-stability assumption below then relates this multiplier to its full-sample counterpart.

We first execute the original emitted inferential program pq​(⋅)p_{q}(\cdot), held fixed throughout the correction, on each subsample. This gives the p-values

pq(1),pq(2),…p_{q}^{(1)},p_{q}^{(2)},\ldots

for the same fixed analysis qq. For a threshold u∈(0,1)u\in(0,1), we assign a subsample D′D^{\prime} to the tail stratum if pq​(D′)≤up_{q}(D^{\prime})\leq u and to the body stratum if pq​(D′)>up_{q}(D^{\prime})>u. For the final correction, we set u=pq​(Dn)u=p_{q}(D_{n}), where DnD_{n} is the observed full dataset.

Within each stratum, we replay the agent once on each subsample, in the order in which the subsamples were drawn. Each replay starts with the original prompt rr and independent agent randomness. We record whether the replay selects the same analysis q=(ℳq,H0,q)q=(\mathcal{M}_{q},H_{0,q}) as the original run.

Recall that

a1,q​(u)=Pr⁡(Q=q∣pq​(D)≤u),a0,q​(u)=Pr⁡(Q=q∣pq​(D)>u),a_{1,q}(u)=\Pr\!\left(Q=q\mid p_{q}(D)\leq u\right),\qquad a_{0,q}(u)=\Pr\!\left(Q=q\mid p_{q}(D)>u\right),

and

Hq​(u)=u​a1,q​(u)u​a1,q​(u)+(1−u)​a0,q​(u).H_{q}(u)=\frac{ua_{1,q}(u)}{ua_{1,q}(u)+(1-u)a_{0,q}(u)}.

Thus, to estimate Hq​(u)H_{q}(u), we only need to estimate the probability that the coding agent selects qq in the favorable tail and in the remaining body of the distribution of pq​(D)p_{q}(D).

Let B1≥1B_{1}\geq 1 and B0≥1B_{0}\geq 1 denote the numbers of coding-agent replays in the tail and body strata, respectively, with total replay budget B=B1+B0B=B_{1}+B_{0}. We draw subsamples until the tail contains B1B_{1} and the body B0B_{0} of them. Subsamples that fall into a stratum after it is full are discarded. We then estimate,

a^1,q(u)=1B1∑b=1B1𝟏{Q1(b)=q},a^0,q(u)=1B0∑b=1B0𝟏{Q0(b)=q},\widehat{a}_{1,q}(u)=\frac{1}{B_{1}}\sum_{b=1}^{B_{1}}\mathbf{1}\left\{Q_{1}^{(b)}=q\right\},\qquad\widehat{a}_{0,q}(u)=\frac{1}{B_{0}}\sum_{b=1}^{B_{0}}\mathbf{1}\left\{Q_{0}^{(b)}=q\right\}, (7)

where Q1(b)Q_{1}^{(b)} denotes a replay on a subsample with pq​(D)≤up_{q}(D)\leq u and Q0(b)Q_{0}^{(b)} a replay on a subsample with pq​(D)>up_{q}(D)>u. We can then estimate

H^q​(u)=u​a^1,q​(u)u​a^1,q​(u)+(1−u)​a^0,q​(u).\widehat{H}_{q}(u)=\frac{u\widehat{a}_{1,q}(u)}{u\widehat{a}_{1,q}(u)+(1-u)\widehat{a}_{0,q}(u)}. (8)

Evaluating this plug-in estimator at the observed p-value u=pq​(Dn)u=p_{q}(D_{n}) gives the estimated selective p-value

p^qsel=H^q​(u).\widehat{p}_{q}^{\mathrm{sel}}=\widehat{H}_{q}(u).

The corresponding estimate of the selection multiplier is

λ^q​(u)=H^q​(u)u,u∈(0,1).\widehat{\lambda}_{q}(u)=\frac{\widehat{H}_{q}(u)}{u},\qquad u\in(0,1). (9)

These expressions require at least one replay in each stratum and a positive denominator in (8). If either stratum has no replay, or the denominator is zero, we report the correction as unavailable. For the mathematical definition of the test, we set p^qsel=1\widehat{p}_{q}^{\mathrm{sel}}=1 on these outcomes.

The most expensive step of the procedure is agent replays. An agent can try many things when selecting an analysis, which can lead to highly skewed ratios of selection to execution compute time: in some of our experiments, the agent took up to 157,000157{,}000 times as long to select an analysis as it took to execute the selected analysis code. Also, coding agents typically incur monetary cost in the form of tokens. It therefore matters how a fixed budget BB is divided between the tail and body, i.e., how B1B_{1} and B0B_{0} are chosen. Because running the code is cheap, we can execute it on every subsample drawn and sort the subsamples into strata before spending agent calls.

To guide allocation, we approximate the replay indicators within each stratum as independent Bernoulli variables with success probability as,q​(u)a_{s,q}(u) in stratum s∈{0,1}s\in\{0,1\}, and treat the two strata as independent. At a fixed threshold uu, the delta method gives the following approximation to the variance due to replay sampling:

Var⁡{H^q​(u)}≈(u⁡(1−u)​a0,q​(u)ρq​(u)2)2​a1,q​(u)​{1−a1,q​(u)}B1+(u⁡(1−u)​a1,q​(u)ρq​(u)2)2​a0,q​(u)​{1−a0,q​(u)}B0,\operatorname{Var}\!\left\{\widehat{H}_{q}(u)\right\}\approx\left(\frac{u(1-u)a_{0,q}(u)}{\rho_{q}(u)^{2}}\right)^{2}\frac{a_{1,q}(u)\{1-a_{1,q}(u)\}}{B_{1}}+\left(\frac{u(1-u)a_{1,q}(u)}{\rho_{q}(u)^{2}}\right)^{2}\frac{a_{0,q}(u)\{1-a_{0,q}(u)\}}{B_{0}},

where

ρq​(u)=u​a1,q​(u)+(1−u)​a0,q​(u).\rho_{q}(u)=ua_{1,q}(u)+(1-u)a_{0,q}(u).

For a fixed total number of replays B=B1+B0B=B_{1}+B_{0} and 0<as,q​(u)<10<a_{s,q}(u)<1, minimizing this variance approximation over positive continuous allocations gives the Neyman allocation (Neyman, 1934),

B1B0=a0,q​(u)​{1−a1,q​(u)}a1,q​(u)​{1−a0,q​(u)}.\frac{B_{1}}{B_{0}}=\sqrt{\frac{a_{0,q}(u)\{1-a_{1,q}(u)\}}{a_{1,q}(u)\{1-a_{0,q}(u)\}}}.

Since the selection probabilities are unknown, we first estimate them using a pilot batch of replays in each stratum and substitute these estimates into the allocation rule. For allocation purposes only, we regularize the pilot proportions to lie strictly between zero and one. We impose minimum replay counts Bs≥bmin​(B)B_{s}\geq b_{\min}(B), s=0,1s=0,1, where bmin​(B)→∞b_{\min}(B)\to\infty and bmin​(B)/B→0b_{\min}(B)/B\to 0. These constraints ensure that neither stratum receives only a fixed number of replays as the total budget grows. The pilot replays serve only to choose the allocation but not to compute the estimated correction or its confidence bands (see below). In our experiments, this simple rule reduced the number of agent replays required for an equal amount of precision by a factor of three to five.

2.2.2 Resampling datasets

A crucial ingredient of the estimator is the resampled datasets on which we replay the agent. Since a coding agent can inspect any aspect of its inputs, its selection behavior could respond to practically any statistic of the data, beyond just the pp-value. For example, sampling with replacement can repeat sampling units and thereby change the agent’s behavior. We therefore use subsampling without replacement (Politis and Romano, 1994).

Subsampling has two useful properties for our setting. First, under i.i.d. sampling units, a uniformly selected subsample has exactly the same unconditional distribution as a fresh dataset of mm distinct units. Second, although conditioning on the original selection can distort the distribution of the parent dataset, we can bound the resulting distortion in the subsample distribution, and show that it vanishes as m/n→0m/n\to 0, see Proposition 1 below.

The total variation distance as the worst-case change in selection behavior.

To see the challenge more formally, let Dn=(O1,…,On)∼PnD_{n}=(O_{1},\ldots,O_{n})\sim P^{n}. Because the coding agent can inspect the entire dataset it receives, we need a notion of resampling fidelity that controls not just a particular statistic, but any arbitrary downstream behavior of the agent. The total variation distance—the “testing metric”—provides exactly such a measure. Recall that for any two probability laws 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} and 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2},

dTV​(𝒫1,𝒫2)=sup0≤f≤1|𝔼𝒫1​[f⁡(D)]−𝔼𝒫2​[f⁡(D)]|,d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2})=\sup_{0\leq f\leq 1}\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}[f(D)]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}[f(D)]\right|,

where the supremum is taken over all measurable functions ff with values in [0,1][0,1]. For a fixed analysis qq, define

sq​(d)=Pr⁡(Q=q∣D=d),s_{q}(d)=\Pr(Q=q\mid D=d),

the probability that the coding agent selects qq when presented with dataset dd. Since sq​(d)∈[0,1]s_{q}(d)\in[0,1], it follows immediately that, for any two probability laws 𝒫1\mathcal{P}_{1} and 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} over complete datasets supplied to the coding agent,

|Pr𝒫1⁡(Q=q)−Pr𝒫2⁡(Q=q)|=|𝔼𝒫1​[sq​(D)]−𝔼𝒫2​[sq​(D)]|≤dTV​(𝒫1,𝒫2).\left|\Pr_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}(Q=q)-\Pr_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(Q=q)\right|=\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}[s_{q}(D)]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}[s_{q}(D)]\right|\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2}).

Moreover, if the coding agent is allowed to implement an arbitrary randomized measurable selection rule, then any measurable function ff with values in [0,1][0,1] can be realized as a selection probability for some analysis qq. Hence,

sup𝒜,q|Pr𝒫1⁡(Q=q)−Pr𝒫2⁡(Q=q)|=dTV​(𝒫1,𝒫2).\sup_{\mathcal{A},q}\left|\Pr_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}(Q=q)-\Pr_{\mathcal{P}_{2}}(Q=q)\right|=d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2}).

Thus, the total variation distance is exactly the worst-case change in the coding agent’s selection behavior induced by replacing one dataset law with another.

Bootstrap vs subsampling.

With this in hand, we compare the marginal distribution of a bootstrap dataset with that of a fresh dataset. Let Dm∗D_{m}^{*} denote an mm-out-of-nn bootstrap sample obtained by drawing m≤nm\leq n observations with replacement from Dn=(O1,…,On)∼PnD_{n}=(O_{1},\ldots,O_{n})\sim P^{n}, and suppose that PP is nonatomic. Here, the unconditional distribution averages over both the original sample and the bootstrap indices. There are nmn^{m} possible ordered sequences of bootstrap indices, of which m!​(nm)m!\binom{n}{m} contain only distinct indices. Hence,

Pr⁡(all bootstrap draws are distinct)=m!​(nm)nm.\Pr\left(\text{all bootstrap draws are distinct}\right)=\frac{m!\binom{n}{m}}{n^{m}}.

Whenever at least one bootstrap index is repeated, the bootstrap produces a type of dataset that would occur with probability zero under a truly fresh draw from PmP^{m}. Conditional on all bootstrapped indices being distinct, by contrast, the bootstrap dataset has distribution exactly PmP^{m}. This gives, by the definition of the TV distance,

dTV​(ℒ⁡(Dm∗),Pm)=1−m!​(nm)nm.d_{\mathrm{TV}}\left(\mathcal{L}(D_{m}^{*}),P^{m}\right)=1-\frac{m!\binom{n}{m}}{n^{m}}. (10)

Thus, the total variation discrepancy is exactly the probability that sampling with replacement produces at least one duplicated sampling unit. In particular, for the ordinary nn-out-of-nn bootstrap,

dTV​(ℒ⁡(Dn∗),Pn)=1−n!nn⟶1,d_{\mathrm{TV}}\left(\mathcal{L}(D_{n}^{*}),P^{n}\right)=1-\frac{n!}{n^{n}}\longrightarrow 1,

so the total variation distance converges to one. This establishes a worst-case discrepancy for unrestricted selection rules and of course does not imply that every coding agent reacts to bootstrap duplicates, though in our simulations we frequently noticed agents reacting to unusual features of the data when they appeared.

Subsampling without replacement avoids this duplicated-index effect. If SmS_{m} is a uniformly random subset of mm distinct indices, chosen independently of DnD_{n}, then

ℒ⁡(DSm)=Pm\mathcal{L}(D_{S_{m}})=P^{m}

exactly. This identity is marginal over the original sample and the subsampling indices. It does not assert that resampling from a fixed observed dataset produces independent fresh draws from PmP^{m}.

Two more issues remain, however, driven by the fact that we resample from the single observed “parent” dataset DnD_{n}.

First, conditional on the analysis qq being selected, the law of the observed dataset DnD_{n} is not necessarily equal to PnP^{n}, which represents the ex-ante distribution of the datasets. That is, we have,

ℒ⁡(Dn∣Q=q)≠Pn.\mathcal{L}(D_{n}\mid Q=q)\neq P^{n}.

Intuitively, observing the agent select analysis qq tells us something about the data DnD_{n}, in particular, that it is more likely to have features that made qq an attractive analysis to the agent. Subsamples of the original dataset may therefore inherit some of these features and, as a result, not behave like typical datasets drawn from PmP^{m}.

Second, even absent selection, all subsamples are drawn from the same observed parent dataset DnD_{n}. If the subsampling indices are drawn independently across subsamples, these datasets are independent conditional on DnD_{n}, but generally dependent unconditionally. Increasing the number of subsamples therefore approximates the resampling distribution associated with the observed DnD_{n}. However, it does not directly establish the convergence to the corresponding population quantities under PmP^{m}. That step needs a separate concentration argument as nn grows.

The following proposition bounds the distortion caused by conditioning on the original selection event. We impose the following sampling assumption.

Assumption 1 (Subsampling).

The observed dataset Dn=(O1,…,On)∼PnD_{n}=(O_{1},\dots,O_{n})\sim P^{n} consists of nn i.i.d. sampling units. Each subsample DSmD_{S_{m}} is constructed by selecting a uniformly random subset of mm distinct indices from {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} and placing the selected units in a uniformly random order. These index selections and orderings are independent across subsamples and independent of DnD_{n} and the agent’s randomness Ξ\Xi. Each agent replay uses fresh, independent randomness.

Proposition 1 (Subsampling bounds the selection contamination).

Let ρq,n≔Pr⁡(Q=q)>0\rho_{q,n}\coloneqq\Pr(Q=q)>0. Then, under Assumption 1,

dTV​(ℒ⁡(DSm∣Q=q),Pm)≤m2​n​log⁡1ρq,n.d_{\mathrm{TV}}\left(\mathcal{L}(D_{S_{m}}\mid Q=q),P^{m}\right)\leq\sqrt{\frac{m}{2n}\log\frac{1}{\rho_{q,n}}}.

Hence, whenever

mn​log⁡1ρq,n→0,\frac{m}{n}\log\frac{1}{\rho_{q,n}}\to 0,

the conditional law of a random size-mm subsample from a dataset that induced selection of qq approaches the fresh-data law PmP^{m} in total variation. Under the recurrence assumption imposed below (Assumption 5), which keeps ρq,n\rho_{q,n} bounded away from zero, this condition is implied by the standard subsampling condition m/n→0m/n\to 0. Otherwise, if the selection probability vanishes, the condition requires its rate to be controlled relative to the subsample size.

This bound controls the distortion caused by conditioning on the original selection event. Convergence of averages computed from subsamples sharing the same parent dataset requires an additional, standard concentration argument, which we provide below.

In practice, subsampling requires specifying sampling units that satisfy Assumption 1. We assume that the research design provides enough information for the researcher, or a helper coding agent, to identify these units. In an i.i.d. cross section, each sampling unit can simply be an observation. In clustered or panel settings, each sampling unit can instead comprise an entire cluster or a panel unit’s full sequence of observations, provided these units are i.i.d. Dependence within a clustered sampling unit is allowed, since its observations are kept together when subsampling. Dependence across sampling units, as in time series or spatial data, is outside the scope of this paper. An extension using, for example, block subsampling would require additional assumptions and a separate validity argument.

2.2.3 Measuring selection

Estimating the selection probabilities requires identifying whether each replay agent selects the same analysis q∗=(ℳq∗,H0,q∗)q^{*}=(\mathcal{M}_{q^{*}},H_{0,q^{*}}) as the original agent. In a typical agentic workflow, the agent can provide a textual summary, numerical results, and code without explicitly stating its statistical model and null hypothesis. Even when it states both, different runs may express the same analysis using different notation, variable names, or textual descriptions. Therefore, requiring an exact match based on the agent’s full outputs is far too restrictive to be of practical use.

Our matching step therefore compares the statistical content of the reported analyses, ignoring purely representational differences. Two runs match if they report the same statistical model, including the same target population and outcome, and the same null hypothesis. The code and sequence of exploratory steps can then be different between the runs.

The commitment prompt.

To implement this matching step, we exploit the fact that coding agents are promptable. After each run has completed its analysis, we append a fixed commitment prompt asking the agent to state, in a self-contained manner, the statistical model and null hypothesis used in that analysis. The prompt asks the agent to describe the completed analysis without revising it. This reporting step is considered to be included in the selection mapping 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} and is applied in the same way to the original run and every replay.

Each replay agent first commits to its own analysis q′q^{\prime}. After an agent commits, we provide the original agent’s description of q∗q^{*} and append a fixed comparison prompt. This prompt asks whether the two descriptions specify the same statistical model and null hypothesis, ignoring purely representational differences such as notation or variable relabeling. The comparison leaves the committed analysis q′q^{\prime} unchanged and produces a binary match decision.

This protocol allows agents to describe their analyses without imposing a common notation or a fixed catalogue of possible analyses. Our use of comparative prompting is motivated by work on LLMs as judges (Zheng et al., 2023, see, e.g.). Under the reporting and matching assumptions stated below, the binary response identifies the event Q′=q∗Q^{\prime}=q^{*}, which is all that our method requires.

The below assumption formalizes what is required for this approach to accurately measure the target event {Q′=q∗}\{Q^{\prime}=q^{*}\}: truthful reporting by the agent.

Assumption 2 (Trust your agent).

Under the data-generating and replay laws considered in this paper, the following statements hold almost surely.

  1. (i)

    Correct implementation. Whenever the procedure evaluates an analysis qq on a dataset D′D^{\prime}, the emitted code returns the fixed pp-value pq​(D′)p_{q}(D^{\prime}). This applies to the original dataset and to execution of the original program on subsamples.

  2. (ii)

    Faithful reporting. The commitment report accurately states the statistical model and null hypothesis selected and implemented by the agent.

  3. (iii)

    Correct matching. For a replay selecting Q′=𝒜r​(D′,Ξ′)Q^{\prime}=\mathcal{A}_{r}(D^{\prime},\Xi^{\prime}), the binary comparison response I′I^{\prime} satisfies

    I′=𝟏{Q′=q∗},I^{\prime}=\mathbf{1}\{Q^{\prime}=q^{*}\},

    where q∗q^{*} is the originally selected analysis.

Our validity results below take these accuracy assumptions as given. The phrase trust your agent reflects a basic premise of delegating empirical work: an agent trusted to carry out an analysis should also be able to accurately explain what it has done and to compare it against other analyses.

Under Assumption 2, the replay procedure identifies selection through the reported model and null hypothesis, not through the code the agent emits. The selection correction focuses on addressing the effect of choosing qq adaptively from the data. Implementation errors, inaccurate reports, and errors in matching are outside the scope of the present guarantees. Assessing and relaxing these accuracy assumptions is complementary to work on agent evaluation and verification (Gu et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025; Majumder et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Candès et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026, see, e.g.). In practice, if the researcher is using a lower-quality AI model as their analysis agent, we recommend having a higher-quality agent review its matching declarations.

2.2.4 Summary

Figure 2 summarizes the proposed procedure. In the “Original Analysis” pane, the researcher provides the agent with a prompt rr, which is chosen independently of the data, and the dataset DnD_{n}. The agent then selects an analysis q∗=(ℳq∗,H0,q∗)q^{*}=(\mathcal{M}_{q^{*}},H_{0,q^{*}}) and reports p∗=pq∗​(Dn)p^{*}=p_{q^{*}}(D_{n}). Because the agent chooses q∗q^{*} based on DnD_{n}, the fixed-analysis calibration of this procedure need not hold conditional on Q=q∗Q=q^{*}. The “Selective Replay” pane thus estimates how much more likely the agent is to select q∗q^{*} on datasets where q∗q^{*} looks at least as favorable as on DnD_{n}.

In the “Selective Replay” pane, we draw subsamples D(1),D(2),…D^{(1)},D^{(2)},\ldots of size m<nm<n using the subsampling scheme from Assumption 1. We execute the original program on each subsample and assign it to a tail stratum, where pq∗​(D(j))≤p∗p_{q^{*}}(D^{(j)})\leq p^{*}, or a body stratum, where pq∗​(D(j))>p∗p_{q^{*}}(D^{(j)})>p^{*}. We keep drawing until the tail contains B1B_{1} subsamples and the body B0B_{0}, and replay the agent once on each, using the original prompt rr and independent agent randomness Ξ′\Xi^{\prime}. The allocation of the B1B_{1} tail and B0B_{0} body replays can be chosen using pilot estimates and the Neyman allocation rule described above. After completing its initial response, each replay agent first commits to its own analysis, after which it is asked to compare its report with the original agent’s report for q∗q^{*} and decide if there is a match.

Under Assumption 2, the recorded matches identify whether each replay selects q∗q^{*}. The estimated tail and body reselection frequencies then yield the correction

p^q∗sel=H^q∗​(p∗).\widehat{p}_{q^{*}}^{\mathrm{sel}}=\widehat{H}_{q^{*}}(p^{*}).

When the correction is unavailable, we follow the non-rejection convention described above. Under the conditions of Theorem 1, the resulting pp-value is asymptotically valid conditional on Q=q∗Q=q^{*}.

2.3 Comparison to existing approaches

Black-box selective inference.

As discussed in the Introduction, our paper builds on a rich literature in conditional selective inference, which aims to restore the statistical guarantees of uncertainty statements about an analysis conditional on it being chosen based on the data. In contrast to most of that literature, the selection rule we study here cannot be characterized, seeing as it is an unknown stochastic mapping from the data to the reported analysis that is implicitly defined by the billions to trillions of parameters of the AI model conducting the analysis. That is, coding agents are black-box selectors.

Markovic et al. (2019) and Liu et al. (2022) also rerun a black-box selector to correct inference, targeting the law of an estimator θ^\widehat{\theta} conditional on selection. Since selection generally also depends on other features of the data, whose law involves unknown nuisance parameters, they assume that the algorithm depends on the data only through a summary statistic specified by the analyst, such as X⊤​yX^{\top}y for the lasso, that is asymptotically jointly Gaussian with θ^\widehat{\theta}. This statistic can then be written as a linear function of θ^\widehat{\theta} plus an independent residual. Conditioning on the residual leaves a selection probability that depends only on θ^\widehat{\theta}, and a Gaussian law for θ^\widehat{\theta} that depends only on θ\theta. They then learn this selection probability, either by rerunning the algorithm on synthetic values of the summary statistic (Markovic et al., 2019) or by fitting a classifier on bootstrapped data (Liu et al., 2022), and reweight the Gaussian law by it. Both methods thus treat the map from a specified statistic to the selected model as a black box. For a coding agent, however, which can respond to any feature of the files it reads, the assumption that selection depends on a low-dimensional summary statistic that is Gaussian is unrealistic, as the only statistic guaranteed to capture its selection is the dataset itself (Section 2.2.2).

More recently, Liu and Panigrahi (2025) proposed a method that allows for arbitrary black-box selection mappings by learning the selection-conditional distribution of an estimator through flow-based transport maps. Their approach relaxes the assumption that the selection mapping has a low-dimensional Gaussian summary, but instead requires the ability to simulate datasets under a suitable null model. For coding agents that can inspect arbitrary features of the data, the null hypothesis attached to the selected analysis generally does not specify the joint distribution of all the data features that may influence selection, making such simulation difficult.

Instead, we take a different approach and target the pp-value of the selected null hypothesis. Since the null law of a calibrated, fixed-analysis pp-value is asymptotically uniform regardless of the nuisance parameters, we can simply condition only on the selection event and average out all the other information in the data. In particular, we leverage the fact that correcting the reported pp-value requires estimating just two selection probabilities, which condition only on the realization of the original analysis’s pp-value. This averaging in turn only requires being able to sample from the dataset’s generating law, but not from the estimator’s null law. We show that this can be achieved by subsampling from the original dataset, with any remaining influence of the selection event washing out under standard subsampling conditions and asymptotically stable selection. This avoids both the need to summarize the selection mapping through a low-dimensional Gaussian statistic in Markovic et al. (2019); Liu et al. (2022) and the need to specify a full generative null model in Liu and Panigrahi (2025). In exchange, we obtain a test for only a single selected null hypothesis instead of the full selection-conditional distribution of the parameter, though in principle we could also construct confidence sets for the parameter through test inversion, at higher computational cost (Sood, 2024).

Agentic empirical science.

The paper closest to ours in the emerging statistical literature on coding agents is Miao et al. (2026). That paper studies how different prompts affect the distribution of analyses that coding agents consider, and then proposes an “m-value” that reflects how extreme a given analysis produced by a coding agent is relative to this distribution of analyses, on the same dataset. In our notation, let dd denote the observed data, Tq​(d)T_{q}(d) a scalar statistic reported by analysis qq, and Π\Pi a reference distribution over analyses. Then, for the original analysis q∗q^{*}, the (two-sided) m-value they propose is,

mΠ​(q∗,d)=2​min⁡{Prq′∼Π⁡(Tq′​(d)≤Tq∗​(d)),Prq′∼Π⁡(Tq′​(d)≥Tq∗​(d))}.m_{\Pi}\left(q^{*};d\right)=2\min\left\{\operatorname{Pr}_{q^{\prime}\sim\Pi}\left(T_{q^{\prime}}(d)\leq T_{q^{*}}(d)\right),\operatorname{Pr}_{q^{\prime}\sim\Pi}\left(T_{q^{\prime}}(d)\geq T_{q^{*}}(d)\right)\right\}.

In practice, the authors estimate this quantity by an “agentic bootstrap”, which replays coding agents with various prompts r′r^{\prime} (e.g. pro, anti, and neutral immigration personas), logs all the analyses considered by the replayed agents, and constructs an estimate Π^\hat{\Pi} of the reference distribution based on that. Their m-value then measures the atypicality of q∗q^{*} relative to this constructed distribution. An important pitfall of this approach, as noted by the authors as well, is that the mm-value is endogenous to the reference distribution. For example, adding an “extremely anti-immigration” persona to the set of prompts could shift the reference distribution toward more negative estimates and assign previously atypical anti-immigration results non-significant mm-values, even when neither the reported analyses nor the underlying data have changed. Additionally, a significant mm-value indicates that a result is atypical relative to the reference distribution, but does not establish whether that result provides statistically compelling evidence against its own null hypothesis.

By contrast, we hold the original prompt rr and the agent configuration fixed but vary the data to ask instead how the agent’s selection of q∗q^{*} distorts the distribution of its reported pp-value under the null. This yields a method to correct this distortion and restore the validity of statistical inference conditional on having selected q∗q^{*}, following the selective inference literature. Importantly, our method does not require constructing a reference distribution but rather treats the distribution under the original null as the reference, approximating it by resampling the data. The distribution of alternative analyses is left unspecified, as we only need to know whether the agent selected an alternative analysis, but do not need to know or explicitly model this alternative analysis space. Also, as we point out below, our method only depends on minimal assumptions about how agents behave, whereas the mm-value assumes that one can trace out the distribution of possible analyses through injecting contrasting personas in prompts. As we show below, it appears that the latest generation of models has become robust to such persona-based steering.

3 Statistical Results

In this section, we establish the statistical properties of our agentic selection-correction estimator. Throughout this section, we will make the sample-size index explicit in our notation. The subsamples have size m=mnm=m_{n}, where mn→∞m_{n}\rightarrow\infty and mn/n→0m_{n}/n\rightarrow 0 as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. For a generic sample size kk and a fresh dataset Dk∼PkD_{k}\sim P^{k}, let

Uq,k:=pq​(Dk),Qk:=𝒜r​(Dk,Ξ),ρq,k:=PrP⁡(Qk=q),U_{q,k}:=p_{q}(D_{k}),\qquad Q_{k}:=\mathcal{A}_{r}(D_{k},\Xi),\qquad\rho_{q,k}:=\Pr_{P}(Q_{k}=q),

and define the fixed-analysis cdf

Fq,k​(u):=PrP⁡(Uq,k≤u).F_{q,k}(u):=\Pr_{P}(U_{q,k}\leq u).

Whenever ρq,k>0\rho_{q,k}>0, define the conditional cdf

Hq,k​(u):=PrP⁡(Uq,k≤u∣Qk=q).H_{q,k}(u):=\Pr_{P}(U_{q,k}\leq u\mid Q_{k}=q).

Whenever both ρq,k>0\rho_{q,k}>0 and Fq,k​(u)>0F_{q,k}(u)>0, define the selection multiplier

λq,k​(u):=PrP⁡(Qk=q∣Uq,k≤u)ρq,k.\lambda_{q,k}(u):=\frac{\Pr_{P}(Q_{k}=q\mid U_{q,k}\leq u)}{\rho_{q,k}}. (11)

Below, we evaluate these objects at k=mnk=m_{n} and k=nk=n.

3.1 Assumptions

We impose the following assumptions, in addition to Assumptions 1 and 2. They restrict the calibration of the fixed inferential procedure and the behavior of the selection process across datasets and sample sizes.

Assumption 3 (Asymptotic exact calibration).

For the fixed analysis qq under consideration and every P∈𝒫0,qP\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q},

supu∈[0,1]|Fq,k​(u)−u|⟶0as ​k→∞.\sup_{u\in[0,1]}\left|F_{q,k}(u)-u\right|\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{as }k\to\infty.

This assumption requires the fixed-analysis pp-value pq​(Dk)p_{q}(D_{k}) to converge in distribution to Unif⁡(0,1)\operatorname{Unif}(0,1) under each null law P∈𝒫0,qP\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q}. Note that it does permit departures from exact calibration in finite samples. Two-sided t-tests of regression coefficients, Wald tests, tests based on GMM, and bootstrap tests all satisfy Assumption 3 under standard regularity conditions. The assumption concerns only the procedure associated with the fixed analysis qq and places no restriction on the agent’s selection behavior.

Assumption 4 (Selection stability).

The selection multiplier λq,k​(u)\lambda_{q,k}(u) satisfies one of the following conditions:

  1. (a)

    One-sided stability. For the subsample sequence mn→∞m_{n}\to\infty with mn/n→0m_{n}/n\to 0, for every u∈(0,1]u\in(0,1],

    [λq,n​(u)−λq,mn​(u)]+⟶0.\left[\lambda_{q,n}(u)-\lambda_{q,m_{n}}(u)\right]_{+}\longrightarrow 0.
  2. (b)

    Two-sided stability. Under the same subsample sequence, for every u∈(0,1]u\in(0,1],

    |λq,n​(u)−λq,mn​(u)|⟶0.\left|\lambda_{q,n}(u)-\lambda_{q,m_{n}}(u)\right|\longrightarrow 0.

The multiplier compares the probability of selecting qq on datasets where its fixed-analysis pp-value is at most uu with the unconditional probability of selecting qq. This assumption restricts how that relative probability can change between sample sizes mm and nn, while allowing ρq,k\rho_{q,k} to vary with kk.

Condition (a) allows the subsample multiplier to exceed the full-sample multiplier, but requires any excess in the opposite direction to vanish asymptotically. Under the remaining conditions of Theorem 1, this one-sided condition is sufficient for asymptotic validity. Replacing the positive part in (a) with |λq,n​(u)−λq,mn​(u)||\lambda_{q,n}(u)-\lambda_{q,m_{n}}(u)| gives the two-sided stability in (b) and, together with those conditions, asymptotic exactness. Both conditions are imposed pointwise for each null law P∈𝒫0,qP\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q}. See Section 3.3 for a discussion of uniform validity.

Assumption 5 (Recurrence).

For the fixed analysis qq under consideration, there exists ρ⋆>0\rho_{\star}>0 such that, for all nn along the sequence under consideration,

min⁡{ρq,n,ρq,mn}≥ρ⋆.\min\{\rho_{q,n},\rho_{q,m_{n}}\}\geq\rho_{\star}.

This assumption keeps the probability of selecting qq bounded away from zero at both the full-sample size nn and the subsample size mnm_{n}, which is needed so that we can use simple subsampling. This assumption is a restriction on the selected analysis and the agent, not a universal property of coding agents. A well-defined and circumscribed prompt can make this condition more plausible by limiting the range of analyses the agent considers, but does not guarantee it.

By contrast, an open-ended prompt such as “find me something interesting” could lead the agent to select among many different analyses, making any particular qq difficult to reproduce. When selection is very rare, obtaining informative replay estimates may require many agent executions. Cases where the selection probabilities vanish with sample size are excluded by Assumption 5.

3.2 Validity of the replay correction

We first establish the “oracle” validity of the selective pp-value, assuming that the conditional cdf Hq,nH_{q,n} is known under the null law PP. The finite-sample statement follows from applying the cdf transform under the conditional law given Qn=qQ_{n}=q; see also Sood (2024) for related pp-value-based selective corrections.

Proposition 2 (Corrected p-value: oracle validity).

Fix an analysis qq and a law P∈𝒫0,qP\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q}. For every nn for which ρq,n>0\rho_{q,n}>0,

PrP⁡(Hq,n​(Uq,n)≤α∣Qn=q)≤α,α∈[0,1].\Pr_{P}\!\left(H_{q,n}(U_{q,n})\leq\alpha\mid Q_{n}=q\right)\leq\alpha,\qquad\alpha\in[0,1].

Moreover, under Assumptions 3 and 5,

Hq,n​(Uq,n)|Qn=q→𝑑Unif⁡(0,1)as ​n→∞.H_{q,n}(U_{q,n})\mid Q_{n}=q\xrightarrow{d}\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty.

The oracle correction is the cdf transform applied to the distribution conditional on selection. The finite-sample inequality holds even when this distribution is discrete. When Hq,nH_{q,n} is continuous, the corrected pp-value is exactly uniform conditional on the selection. More generally, asymptotic exact calibration of the original pp-value, together with the selection probability being bounded away from zero, gives the stated asymptotic exactness. Note that apart from recurrence, this oracle result places no restriction on the agent’s selection behavior.

Next, we study the asymptotic validity of the estimated correction. Write un=Uq,nu_{n}=U_{q,n}. Recall that a^1,q​(un)\widehat{a}_{1,q}(u_{n}) and a^0,q​(un)\widehat{a}_{0,q}(u_{n}) estimate the probabilities of re-selecting qq in the tail and body strata, respectively. Whenever both replay frequencies are defined and the denominator is positive, the estimator of the selective pp-value is

p^q,nsel:=un​a^1,q​(un)un​a^1,q​(un)+(1−un)​a^0,q​(un).\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}:=\frac{u_{n}\widehat{a}_{1,q}(u_{n})}{u_{n}\widehat{a}_{1,q}(u_{n})+(1-u_{n})\widehat{a}_{0,q}(u_{n})}. (12)

Otherwise, we set p^q,nsel=1\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}=1, following the convention of Section 2.2.1.

Theorem 1 (Estimated selective p-value: asymptotic validity).

Fix an analysis qq and a law P∈𝒫0,qP\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q} and suppose Assumptions 1, 2, 3, 4(a), and 5 hold. Let mn→∞m_{n}\to\infty with mn/n→0m_{n}/n\to 0. Draw subsamples as in Assumption 1 until the tail and body strata contain B1,nB_{1,n} and B0,nB_{0,n} subsamples, and replay the agent once on each. Use fresh agent randomness Ξ′\Xi^{\prime} that is i.i.d. across replays and independent of DnD_{n}, the original randomness Ξ\Xi, and the subsample draws. The replay counts can be chosen adaptively, but must satisfy

Bs,n⟶p∞,s∈{0,1},B_{s,n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}\infty,\quad s\in\{0,1\},

under the conditional law given Qn=qQ_{n}=q. Let p^q,nsel\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}} be the estimator in (12).

Then, for every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

lim supn→∞PrP⁡(p^q,nsel≤α∣Qn=q)≤α.\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{P}\!\left(\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}\leq\alpha\mid Q_{n}=q\right)\leq\alpha. (13)

If additionally Assumption 4(b) holds, then, writing un=Uq,nu_{n}=U_{q,n},

p^q,nsel−Hq,n​(un)⟶p0,λ^q​(un)−λq,n​(un)⟶p0,\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}-H_{q,n}(u_{n})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}0,\qquad\widehat{\lambda}_{q}(u_{n})-\lambda_{q,n}(u_{n})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}0, (14)

conditional on Qn=qQ_{n}=q, where λ^q​(un)=p^q,nsel/un\widehat{\lambda}_{q}(u_{n})=\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}/u_{n}. In particular,

p^q,nsel|Qn=q→𝑑Unif⁡(0,1).\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}\mid Q_{n}=q\xrightarrow{d}\operatorname{Unif}(0,1).

Theorem 1 establishes that selection probabilities estimated from subsampled replay datasets can provide asymptotically valid inference for the full-sample analysis, conditional on the original agent selecting qq and under the stated assumptions.

Assumption 4(a), which requires the subsample multiplier λq,mn\lambda_{q,m_{n}} to be at least as large in the limit as the full-sample one, λq,n\lambda_{q,n}, gives the asymptotic validity in Eq. (13) because it makes the estimated correction at least as large as the oracle correction in the limit, which is valid by Proposition 2. Under the stronger assumption that the difference between the two multipliers goes to zero (Assumption 4(b)), we get the stronger result in Eq. (14), which implies that the corrected p-value is exactly uniformly distributed in the limit, conditional on Qn=qQ_{n}=q.

3.3 Uniformity over null distributions

Theorem 1 establishes pointwise asymptotic validity for each fixed null distribution PP. To extend this pointwise result to uniform validity, we introduce strengthened assumptions, which ensure that the worst-case conditional size distortion over a prescribed class vanishes as the sample size increases.

Throughout this subsection, we fix an analysis qq and define a nonempty class 𝔓0,q⊆𝒫0,q\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{0,q} of null distributions. The agent, prompt, and fixed-analysis inferential procedure stay unchanged as PP varies. We use superscripts PP to make the dependence of Fq,kPF^{P}_{q,k}, Hq,kPH^{P}_{q,k}, ρq,kP\rho^{P}_{q,k}, and λq,kP\lambda^{P}_{q,k} on the data-generating law explicit.

In order to state the uniform results, we maintain the sampling, implementation, and replay-design conditions of Theorem 1 for every P∈𝔓0,qP\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}. We define mnm_{n} to be a deterministic sequence, which is common to all distributions in this class.

Based on this, we strengthen the calibration, recurrence, selection-stability, and replay-growth conditions as follows.

Assumption 6 (Uniform calibration).

The fixed-analysis p-value satisfies

κn:=supP∈𝔓0,qmax⁡supu∈[0,1]k∈{n,mn}⁡|Fq,kP​(u)−u|→0as ​n→∞.\kappa_{n}:=\sup_{P\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}}\max_{k\in\{n,m_{n}\}}\sup_{u\in[0,1]}\left|F^{P}_{q,k}(u)-u\right|\to 0\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.
Assumption 7 (Uniform recurrence).

There exist ρ⋆>0\rho_{\star}>0 and an integer n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1 such that, for every n≥n0n\geq n_{0},

infP∈𝔓0,qmink∈{n,mn}⁡ρq,kP≥ρ⋆.\inf_{P\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}}\min_{k\in\{n,m_{n}\}}\rho^{P}_{q,k}\geq\rho_{\star}.
Assumption 8 (Uniform selection stability).

The selection multipliers satisfy one of the following conditions:

  1. (a)

    One-sided stability. For every fixed u∈(0,1]u\in(0,1],

    supP∈𝔓0,q[λq,nP​(u)−λq,mnP​(u)]+→0.\sup_{P\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}}\left[\lambda^{P}_{q,n}(u)-\lambda^{P}_{q,m_{n}}(u)\right]_{+}\to 0.
  2. (b)

    Two-sided stability. For every fixed u∈(0,1]u\in(0,1],

    supP∈𝔓0,q|λq,nP​(u)−λq,mnP​(u)|→0.\sup_{P\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}}\left|\lambda^{P}_{q,n}(u)-\lambda^{P}_{q,m_{n}}(u)\right|\to 0.
Assumption 9 (Uniform replay growth).

Let Bs,nB_{s,n} denote the number of completed replays in stratum s∈{0,1}s\in\{0,1\}, with Bs,n=0B_{s,n}=0 when no replay is completed. For every fixed integer M≥1M\geq 1,

supP∈𝔓0,qPrP⁡(mins∈{0,1}⁡Bs,n<M|Qn=q)→0.\sup_{P\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}}\Pr_{P}\!\left(\min_{s\in\{0,1\}}B_{s,n}<M\,\middle|\,Q_{n}=q\right)\to 0.

These conditions are a direct strengthening of the assumptions required for Theorem 1 in that they hold uniformly over the chosen class of null distributions. As is standard for uniformity results, these assumptions are most plausible on a restricted class of null laws for which the inferential procedure satisfies uniform regularity conditions, and under which the features of PP that affect the agent’s selection behavior are well separated relative to the sampling error, as discussed below. Under these assumptions, we have the following uniformity result.

Corollary 1 (Uniform selective validity and exactness).

Suppose Assumptions 1 and 2 hold for every P∈𝔓0,qP\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}, and use the subsampling and within-stratum replay design of Theorem 1. Let mnm_{n} be a deterministic sequence, common to all P∈𝔓0,qP\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}, satisfying

mn→∞,mn/n→0.m_{n}\to\infty,\quad m_{n}/n\to 0.

Let p^q,nsel\widehat{p}^{\mathrm{sel}}_{q,n} be the estimator of Theorem 1, with the same failure convention.

Then, under Assumptions 6, 7, 8(a), and 9,

supP∈𝔓0,qsupα∈[0,1][PrP⁡(p^q,nsel≤α|Qn=q)−α]+→0.\sup_{P\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}}\sup_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\left[\Pr_{P}\!\left(\widehat{p}^{\mathrm{sel}}_{q,n}\leq\alpha\,\middle|\,Q_{n}=q\right)-\alpha\right]_{+}\to 0.

If, in addition, Assumption 8(b) holds, then

supP∈𝔓0,qsupα∈[0,1]|PrP⁡(p^q,nsel≤α|Qn=q)−α|→0.\sup_{P\in\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}}\sup_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\left|\Pr_{P}\!\left(\widehat{p}^{\mathrm{sel}}_{q,n}\leq\alpha\,\middle|\,Q_{n}=q\right)-\alpha\right|\to 0.

Assumption 6 on uniform calibration requires the fixed-analysis p-value to be asymptotically uniform at both sample sizes, with an approximation error that vanishes uniformly over the class of null distributions. Assumption 7 on uniform recurrence requires a common positive lower bound on all selection probabilities within this class. Note in particular that positive selection probabilities for each fixed law do not guarantee such a bound, since the selection probability could tend to zero along a sequence of laws in the class. Finally, Assumption 9 on uniform replay growth requires enough completed replays in both strata, also uniformly over the class. These assumptions are natural uniform analogues of their pointwise counterparts and impose relatively mild requirements on the data-generating process and the replay design.

Assumption 8 is a substantive restriction. It addresses a different problem: whether the correction learned from subsamples stays appropriate for the full sample. The challenge is that the null for qq can leave the effects of competing analyses and nuisance coefficients that influence the agent’s choice completely unrestricted. In regular settings, an effect of order n−1/2n^{-1/2} can influence selection at size nn, while its standardized signal at size mnm_{n} vanishes as mn/n→0\sqrt{m_{n}/n}\to 0. In other words, the same dilution that removes the trace of the original selection on subsamples (Proposition 1) can also erase signals that are relevant to selection. This means that validity for every fixed distribution can coexist with persistent size distortions along sequences of null distributions. This is a known limitation of subsampling (Andrews and Guggenberger, 2010; Romano and Shaikh, 2012, Theorem 2.1).

Intuitively, Assumption 8 requires the subsample correction to be large enough to account for selection in the full sample. More precisely, at every fixed p-value threshold, the subsample multiplier must be at least as large as the full-sample multiplier, up to an error that vanishes uniformly over the null-law class. A larger correction can make the test conservative, which is allowed by the validity conclusion of Corollary 1. If the two multipliers converge to each other uniformly, the corollary instead gives rejection probabilities that converge uniformly to the nominal level.

This still allows the agent to use the data to choose an analysis, but the correction obtained at the smaller sample size has to adequately account for that choice at the full sample size. This does not follow simply because the individual tests are valid, or because the agent considers only true null hypotheses. Increasing the number of replays estimates the subsample correction more accurately, but cannot fix a mismatch between the corrections needed at the two sample sizes.

Assumption 8 is plausible when the features of PP that affect the agent’s selection behavior are well separated relative to their sampling error. It also holds, for example, if the agent responds only to tt-statistics or pp-values whose joint distribution is asymptotically invariant to the sample size.

Remark 1 (Uniformly valid inference procedures).

Failure of Assumption 8 does not rule out uniformly valid inference using other approaches. The main challenge with adopting existing approaches (Andrews and Guggenberger, 2009; McCloskey, 2017, e.g.,) is that it is unknown which nuisance parameters matter to the agent.

3.4 Power

Next, we characterize the asymptotic power of the corrected test implied by the corrected p-value p^q,nsel\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}. For α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), define the corrected test and its oracle counterpart as ϕn,α:=𝟏{p^q,nsel≤α}\phi_{n,\alpha}:=\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}\leq\alpha\} and ϕn,αor:=𝟏{Hq,nP0(Uq,n)≤α}\phi^{\mathrm{or}}_{n,\alpha}:=\mathbf{1}\{H_{q,n}^{P_{0}}(U_{q,n})\leq\alpha\}, respectively, where Hq,nP0H_{q,n}^{P_{0}} is the oracle cdf under a null law P0∈𝒫0,qP_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q} and, by convention, ϕn,α=0\phi_{n,\alpha}=0 whenever the correction is unavailable. We are interested in the power of this test, conditional on the agent selecting qq, that is, PrP⁡(ϕn,α=1∣Qn=q)\Pr_{P}(\phi_{n,\alpha}=1\mid Q_{n}=q).

We need one additional assumption for consistency, which ensures that both strata contain at least one replay. If this assumption does not hold, the proposed correction is unavailable and the test does not reject.

Assumption 10 (Availability of replay observations).

Along the sequence of alternative laws PnP_{n} under consideration, let Bs,nB_{s,n} denote the number of completed agent replays in stratum s∈{0,1}s\in\{0,1\}, with Bs,n=0B_{s,n}=0 when no replay is available in that stratum. We assume that

PrPn⁡(B1,n≥1,B0,n≥1∣Qn=q)⟶1.\Pr_{P_{n}}\!\left(B_{1,n}\geq 1,\;B_{0,n}\geq 1\mid Q_{n}=q\right)\longrightarrow 1.

We can now state the following power and consistency result.

Proposition 3 (Oracle power and consistency).

  1. (a)

    Local alternatives. Fix a null distribution P0∈𝒫0,qP_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q}. Suppose all conditions of Theorem 1 hold under P0P_{0}, with the two-sided selection-stability condition in Assumption 4(b) replacing the one-sided condition in Assumption 4(a). Let PnnP_{n}^{n} be contiguous to P0nP_{0}^{n} and suppose lim infnPrPn⁡(Qn=q)>0\liminf_{n}\Pr_{P_{n}}(Q_{n}=q)>0. Let Hq,nP0H_{q,n}^{P_{0}} denote the oracle cdf under P0P_{0}. Then, for every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

    PrPn⁡(ϕn,α≠ϕn,αor∣Qn=q)⟶0.\Pr_{P_{n}}\!\left(\phi_{n,\alpha}\neq\phi^{\mathrm{or}}_{n,\alpha}\mid Q_{n}=q\right)\longrightarrow 0.
  2. (b)

    Consistency. Under any sequence of alternatives satisfying Assumption 10, suppose that, conditional on Qn=qQ_{n}=q,

    Uq,na^0,q​(Uq,n)⟶p0,\frac{U_{q,n}}{\widehat{a}_{0,q}(U_{q,n})}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}0,

    where the ratio is defined as ∞\infty whenever its denominator is zero. Then

    p^q,nsel⟶p0\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}0

    conditional on Qn=qQ_{n}=q, or equivalently,

    PrPn⁡(ϕn,α=1∣Qn=q)⟶1for every ​α∈(0,1).\Pr_{P_{n}}\!\left(\phi_{n,\alpha}=1\mid Q_{n}=q\right)\longrightarrow 1\qquad\text{for every }\alpha\in(0,1).

Part (a) shows that under contiguous alternatives, the test ϕn,α\phi_{n,\alpha} based on the estimated selective p-value p^q,nsel\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}} has the same asymptotic power as the corresponding “oracle” test ϕn,αor\phi^{\mathrm{or}}_{n,\alpha}. Part (b) shows that ϕn,α\phi_{n,\alpha} inherits consistency from the original p-value as long as both strata contain replays and the agent does not exclusively select the original analysis on subsamples in the favorable tail as the data grows. The latter condition is a version of a recurrence condition, imposed under the alternative on the less favorable subsamples in the body stratum.

3.5 Confidence intervals under finite replay budget

Theorem 1 establishes asymptotic validity of the corrected p-value as the number of replays diverges. Since, in practice, the number of replays is determined by a finite computational budget, we now construct confidence intervals for Hq,n​(un)H_{q,n}(u_{n}) and λq,n​(un)\lambda_{q,n}(u_{n}) that are valid for such a fixed replay budget. The idea is that, conditional on the data, the number of replays that reselect qq in each stratum is distributed as a binomial, so we can construct an exact finite-sample confidence interval for the correction at the subsample level by leveraging classical results on confidence intervals for binomial proportions (Clopper and Pearson, 1934; Berger and Boos, 1994). We then show that the stability Assumption 4 transfers these confidence intervals to the full-sample targets as well.

Write un=Uq,n∈(0,1)u_{n}=U_{q,n}\in(0,1) and m=mnm=m_{n}. Define the stratum selection probabilities under the subsampling law given DnD_{n},

bs,n:=Pr(𝒜r(DSm,Ξ′)=q|Dn, 1{pq(DSm)≤un}=s),s∈{0,1},b_{s,n}:=\Pr\!\left(\mathcal{A}_{r}(D_{S_{m}},\Xi^{\prime})=q\ \middle|\ D_{n},\ \mathbf{1}\{p_{q}(D_{S_{m}})\leq u_{n}\}=s\right),\qquad s\in\{0,1\},

Lemma 1 (Finite-sample validity).

Suppose Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, let B1,B0≥1B_{1},B_{0}\geq 1 be fixed given DnD_{n}, and suppose that both strata have positive probability under the subsampling law given DnD_{n}. Then, for every a∈[0,1]2a\in[0,1]^{2} with un​a1+(1−un)​a0>0u_{n}a_{1}+(1-u_{n})a_{0}>0,
