The bounds are defined for any counts, including X0=0X_{0}=0 or X1=0X_{1}=0, and are computed only at the observed counts and so remain computationally tractable at large replay budgets. Moreover, for γ≤1/2\gamma\leq 1/2, the interval always contains the point estimate p^q,nsel\widehat{p}^{\mathrm{sel}}_{q,n} (see the proof of Theorem 2). Shorter admissible finite-sample valid intervals for this ratio exist (Wang and Shan, 2015), but their computational cost scales with the full sample space instead of the observed counts and only led to modest reductions in interval width in our experiments, so we do not use them. We obtain the following result.

Theorem 2 (Full-sample confidence intervals).

Fix qq and P∈𝒫0,qP\in\mathcal{P}_{0,q}. Suppose Assumptions 1, 2, 3, and 5 hold, mn→∞m_{n}\to\infty with mn/n→0m_{n}/n\to 0, and B1,B0≥1B_{1},B_{0}\geq 1 are fixed integers.

  3. (c)

    Under Assumption 4(b), for every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

    limmin⁡{B0,B1}→∞lim supn→∞PrP⁡(max⁡{diam⁡ℐn,Bp,diam⁡ℐn,Bλ}>ε∣Qn=q)=0.\lim_{\min\{B_{0},B_{1}\}\to\infty}\ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\ \Pr_{P}\!\left(\max\big\{\operatorname{diam}\mathcal{I}^{p}_{n,B},\operatorname{diam}\mathcal{I}^{\lambda}_{n,B}\big\}>\varepsilon\mid Q_{n}=q\right)=0. (18)

Part (a) gives an upper bound on the selection-corrected pp-value and the multiplier. As such, it can be used to conservatively reject the null at level α\alpha whenever p¯n≤α−γ/2\overline{p}_{n}\leq\alpha-\gamma/2, for γ<2​α\gamma<2\alpha, which accounts for both selection and the finite number of replays.11 1 Note that rejecting when p¯n≤α\overline{p}_{n}\leq\alpha yields a test with asymptotic level at most α+γ/2\alpha+\gamma/2 for a fixed number of replays; by part (c) and Theorem 1, its asymptotic level approaches α\alpha as the number of replays grows. Part (b) gives two-sided intervals. The width of these intervals only reflects uncertainty due to the finite number of replays. Approximation errors from subsampling at size mnm_{n}, from conditioning on the selected dataset, and from finite-sample calibration of the fixed-analysis pp-value are shown to vanish as n→∞n\to\infty in the proof, but are not reflected in the width, which is why the results are asymptotic in nn. Part (c) shows that these intervals shrink to zero width as the replay budget grows, which we corroborate in our simulations below.

Remark 2 (Data-dependent replay budgets).

Lemma 1 treats the replay budget as being fixed in advance. In practice, one may want to allocate replays to the two strata based on a pilot, as in the Neyman allocation described in Section 2.2.1 above. Similarly, one may want to keep adding replays until p¯n\overline{p}_{n} falls below some significance level α\alpha. The first practice is a data-dependent allocation, whereas the second is a form of optional stopping. Both can invalidate the fixed-budget guarantee. For the first, one can restore validity by simply discarding the initial pilot draws and only using the post-pilot draws to compute the confidence bands, which we do in practice. For the second approach, one could instead construct time-uniform confidence sequences for the two selection probabilities (Howard et al., 2021; Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024).

4 Simulations

We now implement four simulation designs to study whether our selection correction indeed restores correct coverage in practice. In the first design, the selection mapping is known — and hence not driven by coding agents’ selection — to allow us to study the true coverage of our selection correction; in the other three, the selection is driven by open-ended coding agents, where we can compare the frequency of the original and corrected p-values but do not know the oracle correction or selection mapping.

4.1 Implementation

Throughout the simulation and application sections, we use GPT-6-Luna as the base model through the Codex CLI at high reasoning effort, unless stated otherwise.

All simulation designs and applications follow the procedure of Section 2.2.4. Each replay starts from an identical copy of the original agent’s workspace. The workspace is a folder inside a Linux machine, with Python and R environments, access to the command line, file creation and editing abilities through the Codex CLI, and limited internet access — no web-search tool and explicit instructions to only use the internet to read technical documentation. Each agent is provided with an initial prompt that varies with the specific simulation design and application, see Section D.1 for the full collection of prompts. The only thing that is modified across replays is the dataset, which is replaced by a randomly drawn subsample, and any corresponding statistics. In particular, we also modify any numerical information in the codebook about the data, like descriptions about the sample size. Indeed, in initial experiments, we found that agents noticed discrepancies between the codebook and the subsampled data and spent some of their analysis trying to reconcile them. This aligns with our arguments above that coding agents need to be replayed on “genuine” resampled datasets. The agents only have access to their folder on the machine they run on and cannot see other agents or other folders, so that nothing in the agents’ environment reveals that they are being replayed. Replays that were refused by the model provider were discarded unread and rerun on the same subsample.

4.2 Simulation Designs

Fixed design.

For the known selection mapping, we simulate a data-generating process similar to Example 2. In particular, we draw 400400 datasets with n=1,000n=1{,}000 i.i.d. observations of six independent outcomes drawn from a standard normal distribution. From each outcome’s observations, we then compute the sample mean and construct a z-score using the known standard error to test whether the outcome jj has a mean equal to zero. The corresponding pp-values are independent and uniformly distributed under the null. We model the selection mapping as in Example 2 as picking the smallest pp-value with probability 0.8 and picking a random one with probability 0.2. The exact selected cdf for a nominal p-value of uu then is,

Hq​(u)=0.2​u+0.8​{1−(1−u)6},H_{q}(u)=0.2u+0.8\{1-(1-u)^{6}\}, (19)

which allows us to compute the true selection-corrected p-value.

Based on this DGP, we apply the correction procedure of Section 2.2.4 in the same way as we would to a coding agent. We draw subsets of m=31m=31 observations, evaluate the selected test on each, split them into tail and body using the selected test’s pp-value calculated on the full data, and replay the selector on BB subsets per stratum, for B∈{25,100,400,1000}B\in\{25,100,400,1000\}. A match is then declared if the replayed selector picks the same analysis jj as the “original” selector on the full data.

Open-ended agent design.

To get a better sense of how well our method performs with real coding agents, we simulate 100 datasets from an imaginary randomized control trial for an employment support program. The coding agent is given a codebook with details on the data and experimental design, which describes the following. The program has 2,0002{,}000 participants at four sites, with half of each site’s participants assigned to the program at random. We simulate the following baseline characteristics: baseline age, sex, parenthood, education, household size, employment, earnings, and months unemployed. Additionally, we simulate the following outcome variables, each “measured” 6 and 12 months after the program: employment, weekly hours worked, monthly earnings, a financial-security index, food insecurity, debt in collections, psychological distress, self-rated health, and training enrollment. The full system of equations that we used to generate this data is given in Appendix C.2. Treatment does not affect any of the outcome variables, so all program effects are exactly equal to zero. This allows us to calculate rejection rates under the null hypothesis, even if we cannot characterize the (agents’) selection mapping as we can in the fixed design above.

The agents receive an open-ended prompt (Section D.1) asking them to provide a team with a “compelling, defensible finding to motivate its next study” and encouraging the agent to “explore the data as you see fit”. The codebook provided to the agent broadly specifies the design (least squares of an outcome on the treatment with robust standard errors) but leaves the choice of outcome, follow-up, sample restrictions, and precise regression specification open to the agent.

For each of the 100 datasets, we run the Luna agent once on the full dataset to get the original analysis. Then, we run replay agents on tail and body subsamples of the dataset of size m=200m=200, giving m/n=0.1m/n=0.1. We draw 40+20040+200 and 240+400240+400 tail and body subsamples respectively, to see the impact of increasing the replay size in this setting.

Real data designs.

One issue with simulated data is that its stylized nature might cause particular types of selection behavior that real data would not. To assess this, we also test the agents on data from real papers published in a top economics journal. The papers study: 1) a randomized evaluation of a workplace wellness program’s effects on employee health and productivity (Jones et al., 2019); 2) a randomized evaluation of the effect of a financial information intervention on mothers’ labor supply (Costa-Ramón et al., 2026); and 3) an online survey experiment testing how consumers make ethical purchasing decisions (Kaufmann et al., 2024). For the first two papers, we permute the randomly assigned treatment, similar to a randomization test, to make the null hypothesis of no effect hold true, while holding the other aspects of the data fixed so that it closely resembles the real data. For the third paper, we create a new column in the data given to the coding agent with an imaginary randomized intervention that was not actually implemented, which should similarly have null effects. We chose these papers based on the criteria that they had to be recently published in a top-5 economics journal, have at least 2,0002{,}000 participants with sampling at the individual level (to simplify subsampling), have publicly available replication data, and evaluate a non-canonical experiment (e.g. not the Rand Health study) to mitigate the AI model having memorized some of the results (see also the discussion in Section 5.2 below). The prompt given to the coding agent is nearly identical to the open-ended simulation design above, just dropping the name of the program, so that one prompt serves all three studies (see Section D.1). The codebook contains details on the experimental design of the paper, the variables in the dataset including design variables and outcomes, and a broad description of the intended methods: OLS regressions of an outcome on the treatment indicator and group dummies with robust standard errors. We removed anything that could identify the studies, including proper nouns and open-text answers from study participants, renamed all variables, and changed the study years. Since memorized study results might influence selection, we also checked the logs of all 24,542 original and replay sessions for any mention of the study authors, title, or title paraphrases, but did not find any. Finally, while all three studies had a pre-registration plan, we do not include those in the codebook since it would obstruct the selective behavior that we are trying to model.

For each of the 3 studies, we draw 34 fresh datasets with the treatment permuted. Then, we run the Luna agent on each of the 102 full datasets at their original size, which we call the “original” analyses. For each original analysis, we then draw 40 tail and 200 body subsample datasets from the permuted fresh dataset with a relative subsample size of m/n=0.1m/n=0.1, replay the Luna agent on them, and estimate the corrected pp-value and λ^\widehat{\lambda} together with their confidence bands.

Power design.

Finally, we test the replay test’s power to reject a false null by injecting “true” treatment effects into 200 new simulated randomized control trials from the open-ended agent design above, 100 for each effect size. In particular, we modify the design to let the treatment (the employment support program) increase employment 12 months after the program by 6.2 and 9.6 percentage points in two sets of simulations, to see how our test’s power increases with effect size. The effect sizes were chosen to target 80% and 99% power for a pre-specified test on a regression coefficient of the treatment with employment as the outcome. They correspond to a Cohen’s d (effect over outcome standard deviation) of 0.127 and 0.190, respectively. The employment effect spills over into three other outcomes at 12 months: weekly hours, monthly earnings, and training enrollment. All other outcomes continue to be unaffected by treatment. We compare the rejection frequency of the replay test under this design against the rejection frequency of the pre-specified test, as well as the average rejection frequency of each “original” agent’s program on 4,000 new datasets drawn with the same effect.

4.3 Results

Table 1 collects the results of all four simulation designs, and Figure 3 summarizes the rejection rates of all designs (panel a) and plots the corrected against the reported p-values for the open-ended design (panel b). Without correction, the agents strongly inflate the false rejection rates: reporting a pp-value of less than 0.050.05 for nearly every original analysis. These strikingly high rejection rates occur under relatively mild selection pressure (“the team needs one compelling, defensible finding”) even as the original prompts specifically encourage the agent to “explain your choice” and “discuss the exploratory nature of the finding”.

Panel a in the figure shows that the replay tests correct these rates to close to the nominal level in each design: 4.2% for the fixed design, 5.1% for the open-ended agents, and 5.9% for the real data design pooled across the three papers. The replay test rejects the null when the upper endpoint of the one-sided 95% confidence band around the corrected pp-value lies below 0.05. Since we use many replays per analysis, we compare its rejection rates with the nominal 5% level, which its level approaches as the number of replays grows (footnote 1).

In Figure 3, panel (b), we plot the agent’s reported pp-values against our corrected ones for the open-ended design. The gray dashed diagonal is the 45-degree line and indicates no correction. The dash-dotted diagonal indicates the correction corresponding to a multiplier λ^\widehat{\lambda} of 19, our median estimated multiplier. Red symbols indicate corrected pp-values that still reject the null, whereas blue ones do not reject. The mass of white and gray circles at the top of the panel indicates simulations in which there were either no matches to the original analysis in the tail replays, in the body replays, or in either. For simulations where there are only tail matches, the corrected pp is 11 indicating maximal estimated selection. For simulations with only body matches, the point estimate for the corrected pp is zero but the upper bound of the confidence band can, and so a statistical decision is still possible, as in the hollow red diamond on the plot. In 19 out of 99 analyses, there is neither a tail nor a body match, in which case there is no point estimate and the analysis is shown at p=1p=1.

Looking more closely at the fixed design in Panel A in Table 1, the estimator (computed by simply replaying the selection rule on the subsamples) reaches the same rejection decision as the oracle correction in 96.2% of simulations with 2525 replays, increasing to 99.8% with 1,0001{,}000 replays. The root mean squared error (RMSE) of the corrected pp-value relative to the known truth decreases at roughly B\sqrt{B} rate with BB the number of replays, falling to 0.0190.019 at 1,0001{,}000 replays, and the mean width of the 95% confidence intervals decreases to 0.0690.069. The confidence bands’ coverage of the known oracle correction also decreases with the number of replays, with some slight undercoverage at the larger replay budgets, which likely reflects asymptotic approximation error. The median multiplier λ^\widehat{\lambda} remains stable around 3.53.5 with shrinking confidence bands. Overall, the theory of Section 3.5 appears to be supported by these results.

Panels B–D in Table 1 demonstrate the performance of the estimator when run with a real, frontier coding agent on realistic, open-ended tasks. We ran the replay on 100 datasets in Panel B and on 100 datasets per effect size in Panel D; in each set, the original agent’s code produced an error on one dataset, so we dropped it and report the results from the remaining 99. Panel B, row 2, shows that the correction achieves a near-nominal false rejection rate with enough replays (5.1%) even when the agent engages in near-total selection of significant results, rejecting in 97/99 (98.0% rounded) of simulations. The “Width” column gives the average width of the two-sided 95% confidence bands around the pp-value across simulations. The fairly large width of 0.710.71 partly reflects the fact that we include simulations with only tail matches, whose confidence bands include 11 as their upper endpoint. When dropping those simulations, the mean width drops to 0.440.44 at 640 replays. Even so, the confidence bands are much wider in Panel B than in Panel A, reflecting two things. One, the higher variance of the selection choices made by actual coding agents on an open-ended task. Two, the extreme selection the agents engage in: they rarely reselect the original analysis when it does not deliver a significant pp-value (only 0.29% of body replays). Nonetheless, these wide bands do not prevent our estimator from detecting statistically significant evidence of strong selection, with median multipliers of 1717–1919 (lower confidence bounds 6.96.9–7.27.2).

Moving to Panel C, the agents again report significant results on nearly 100% of simulations on all three real papers’ data, leading to maximally distorted false rejection rates. By contrast, our replay test based on the corrected pp-values achieves a near-nominal false rejection rate of 5.9%5.9\% on the 102102 simulations pooled across the three papers. On the individual papers, the corrected false rejection rates are slightly more variable, between 0.0%0.0\% and 8.8%8.8\%, which is likely due to the smaller number of simulations (34) within each paper. As in Panel B, our estimator detects strong, significant evidence of selection, with median multipliers λ^\widehat{\lambda} of 1010–2222.

Finally, Panel D tests the power properties of our estimator, by injecting a true treatment effect for one of the outcomes in the open-ended agent design from Panel B, employment at 12 months. We run 40+200 replays on each of 99 datasets of this version of the simulated data, excluding the two datasets where the original agents’ code produced an error. We find that the replay test rejects 49.5% of the time for the smaller effect and 87.9% of the time for the larger one, in line with the results of Section 3.4 that establish the consistency of the corrected pp-value. By comparison, the pre-specified test and the original agents’ analyses on new data, which act as an informal power ceiling, reject 78.8% and 67.9% of the time under the smaller effect. The agent’s own pp-value rejects 100% of the time, driven by a mix of false rejection due to selection and true rejection. The original agent’s analysis is a useful benchmark because the agent sometimes chooses outcomes with true null effects, doing so on 12 out of 99 datasets for the smaller effect and 1 out of 99 for the larger effect, when the true effects start attracting the agents’ selection. Conditional on the agent choosing an outcome with a true effect, the replay test’s rejection frequencies rise to 56.3 and 88.8%.

5 Empirical applications

Next, we illustrate our method on datasets from several real empirical applications. We prompt GPT-6-Luna to carry out a variety of realistic empirical workflows while steering it towards a particular direction, either implicitly or explicitly. The implementation details are analogous to the simulations and are described in Section 4.1.

In the first application, we revisit the role of ideological bias in the analysis of immigration-related empirical questions, following Miao et al. (2026) and Borjas and Breznau (2026). In the second, we let the agent estimate a more open-ended version of Example 1, asking it to use a difference-in-differences design to analyze the effect of the minimum wage on employment using the data and general design of Card and Krueger (1994).

5.1 Ideological bias and immigration

Setup.

We apply our method to the “many analysts” re-implementation exercise from Breznau et al. (2022) and Borjas and Breznau (2026). The authors of those papers gave different research teams the same null hypothesis to test: whether more immigration reduces public support for government welfare programs, and an identical dataset, based on an original paper by Brady and Finnigan (2014). They found that the analysts’ results varied widely, from large negative to large positive effects of immigration (Breznau et al., 2022), and that this variation correlated strongly with teams’ reported stance on immigration policy (Borjas and Breznau, 2026). In a recent paper, Miao et al. (2026) revisited this setting with coding agents, prompted to adopt personas with pro- and anti-immigration views, and found large variation in the agents’ reported estimates that mimicked human analyst variation. We revisit this application in light of our selective replay method.

Persona-driven selection (Miao et al., 2026).

We start by attempting to reproduce the results of Miao et al. (2026), estimating the design of the ideology and immigration application in their paper with three different AI models, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and GPT-6-Luna.22 2 We rely on the authors’ replication package on GitHub as well as the description in their paper. In particular, the agents are prompted to adopt personas with neutral and pro- and anti-immigration perspectives. Then, all analyses considered by the agents in their logs that pass methodological checks are collected and standardized to construct a reference distribution of analyses (see Section 2.3 for a more detailed comparison to Miao et al. (2026)). We rerun this exact design, with the same exact prompts as in the authors’ paper, on a corrected version of their data (Appendix C.3 and Table 2). With Sonnet 4.6, we closely replicate the authors’ results that coding agents with different personas tend to report different, persona-aligned results: 13/18 anti-immigration agents find significant, negative effects of immigration on welfare support, while 9/19 pro-immigration agents find significant, positive effects, compared to 12/17 and 9/17 in Miao et al. (2026). The average difference in zz-statistic reported by anti- and pro-immigration agents is −4.5-4.5, compared to a difference of −4.2-4.2 (95% CI [−5.5,−2.9][-5.5,-2.9]) in Supplementary Figure 3c in Miao et al. (2026).33 3 The authors report a difference of −5.7-5.7 in their main text, but the results in this figure instead indicate −4.2-4.2, as read from the figure’s vector graphics. However, when we try to replicate these results on more recent models at a similar tier as Sonnet 4.6, they completely disappear. For both Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, none of the anti- and pro-immigration agents report significant results aligned with their persona. Moreover, the average difference in zz-statistics reported by the anti- and pro-immigration agents is 0.40.4 for Sonnet 5.5 and 0.20.2 for GPT-6-Luna: close to zero and opposite to the agents’ persona alignment. Thus, the finding that coding agents’ analyses can be steered by assigning them different types of personas may not be robust to the improvements in these agents over time. This agrees with another paper by one of the same authors that finds that most findings about LLMs disappear or diminish within 15 months of publication (Queen and Zou, 2026). By contrast, our selective replay method does not require any assumption on how, or even whether, coding agents select, other than that their selection behavior stabilizes asymptotically. Indeed, the same GPT-6-Luna agents that ignore their assigned personas here reported a pp-value below 0.05 on 97 of 99 null datasets when asked for a compelling finding in our open-ended simulation. To better showcase our method’s ability to detect selection when it does happen and correct it, we now turn to a different design where we do observe the agents selecting on these data.

Realistic selection pressure.

Since the persona-driven design above does not appear to induce selection in the most recent generation of coding agents, we instead model a more realistic empirical workflow with explicit selection pressure. In particular, we give GPT-6-Luna a request in the voice of a researcher at a pro-immigration think tank who is preparing a brief for a policy roundtable on the relation between immigration and welfare support by the public and asks the agent to “lead with the most compelling finding” for it (see the prompt in Appendix D.1), with a suggestion to use individual-level OLS regressions of any of the respondents’ answers on their country’s immigration level with some basic controls. The agent is also provided with the data from the papers above, the ISSP Role of Government modules from 1985 to 2016, which has 154,921 respondents in 46 countries, merged with country-level immigration and economic indicators (see Appendix C.3 for a list of variables in the data). As before, the agent has access to a computing environment and the Codex CLI.

Also as before, we run the Luna agent once on the full data to obtain the “original” analysis, and then replay it on subsamples of 16 out of 46 countries (m/n=0.35m/n=0.35), retaining every respondent inside each country, in line with our sampling Assumption 1. We divide subsampled datasets into body and tail by rerunning the original pp-value estimator and then replay the agent on 500500 subsamples in each stratum. The replay agents’ logs give no indication that the agents noticed some countries were missing or that the data were previously used in the papers above. Each replay judged whether its own analysis matched the original after committing to it (Section 2.2.3).

Results.

In its original analysis on the full data, the agent chose to regress support for government responsibility for the unemployed (1 = definitely should not be [its responsibility], 4 = definitely should be, rescaled to a [0,100][0,100] scale) on a measure of the country’s immigrant stock, controlling for a set of socio-economic variables and survey-year indicators. Its main estimate indicated that a 10 percentage-point higher immigrant stock was associated with 4.6 points lower support on the 100-point scale, with p=0.0123p=0.0123 based on standard errors clustered at the country level.

The agent’s logs document how the agent arrived at this analysis: it estimated the same regression specification for each of the six welfare-related outcomes in the data and then chose the unemployment-responsibility outcome because “it has the clearest negative estimate”. The agent makes this choice despite the prompt’s implicit pro-immigration bias, because among the six specifications it tried, all estimates were negative, and it did not search further. In fact, the agent even tried to avoid searching over specifications by scoping its search over the six welfare outcomes at the start of its analysis. After the first regression it estimated, it logged that continuing to evaluate the other regressions was a “breadth check, not a result-driven decision to stop or change the model”.

Despite this apparent self-justification, our estimates in Figure 4 for the selection multiplier λ\lambda and the corrected pp-value show strong and significant evidence of selection (see our discussion of agents’ attempted self-corrections further below as well). λ^=2.42\widehat{\lambda}=2.42, indicating the agent was over two times more likely to select the original analysis when it delivered a significant estimate, with the 95% one-sided confidence band excluding 11. Correspondingly, the agent’s original pp-value of 0.01230.0123 gets corrected upward to p=0.0299p=0.0299. At the same time, the one-sided confidence band for the corrected pp-value still excludes 0.050.05, so the corrected pp-value can still reject the null hypothesis of the estimated regression coefficient being equal to zero. This illustrates that our correction need not always undermine the statistical significance of a result.

Echoing the results for the persona-driven design, 13/20 reruns of the original agent on the full dataset lead with the same original analysis, finding negative effects of immigration even as the prompt attempts to induce pro-immigration bias. Conversely, 11/20 runs with an analogous anti-immigration prompt arrive at the same analysis on the full data. Thus, the persona does not appear to affect what analyses were selected at all, even as our replay method does find significant evidence of selection. To further assess this, we compute the mm-value of Miao et al. (2026), using the full set of analyses considered in all 20 runs of the pro- and anti-immigration agents, as well as 20 neutral agents (see Appendix D.1 for the precise prompts). Among the 811 analyses considered across all the runs, approximately 12% have a zz-statistic less than or equal to the original’s z=−2.63z=-2.63, so using the rule in Miao et al. (2026) that doubles the smallest tail of the reference distribution, their mm-value is 0.230.23. In other words, the original pro-immigration agent’s analysis is unremarkable relative to the analyses considered by other agents with contrasting personas, because the latest coding agent models appear to be more robust to persona-driven steering. Nevertheless, we find that the agents do engage in significant data-driven selection, by testing out various specifications and selecting the more significant ones more frequently. Moreover, our method does not impose any assumptions on the space of possible analyses, but estimates it from the choices the agent actually makes on resampled versions of the data.

5.2 Minimum wages, employment, and difference-in-differences

Setup.

For our second application, we revisit the empirical design of a classic paper in economics that studied how minimum wages affect employment, by Card and Krueger (1994). The paper collected survey data from 410 fast-food restaurants in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, and compared how the employment of New Jersey restaurants changed after an increase in the minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 there, using a difference-in-differences (DiD) design. We provide the agent with a description of the question, the paper’s original data, and a request to answer the question using a DiD design and report the “most statistically compelling finding” among the analyses that can be justified. Thus, this empirical application can be viewed as a thought experiment: “what would Card and Krueger have estimated if they used coding agents to search for significant results?”

As described in Section 4.1, the agent has access to a compute environment and file-write and edit commands as well as limited internet access. The full initial prompt given to the agent is provided in Appendix D.1. We run the agent once on the full dataset, and then replay it on 3,000 random subsamples of 150 restaurants, 1,142 in the tail and 1,858 in the body, following the Neyman allocation rule from Section 2.2.1. The match review classifies 2,985 of these replays (15 remain unresolved); the displays of the replays’ programs use the 2,983 whose final program was recovered, and Figure 7 the 2,944 with a purpose code for every step. Since this is a more complicated analysis task, we verify the claims made by a Luna agent about whether its selected analysis matches the original analysis. In particular, we ask GPT-6.1-Sol (high effort) to compare the model and null hypothesis each replay agent declared with the original analysis’s declaration (see Section D.1 for the review agent’s prompt). As noted above, this allows us to slightly relax the “Trust your agent” assumption 2 for a weaker model like Luna.

The setup as a whole leaves a lot of “researcher degrees of freedom”, even with the relatively well-specified question and empirical design: employment can be measured as full-time-equivalent employees (FTE) or as total headcount; restaurants that dropped out of the second survey wave can be dropped or recoded; and there are many possible choices of what variables to control for in the regression. For a full list of variables in the data, see Table 6.

Results.

The agent, when run on the full dataset, decided to regress the change in nonmanager full-time-equivalent employment on a dummy variable for whether the restaurant is in New Jersey or not, and a set of chain fixed effects, using OLS with HC2 standard errors. The estimate it reported for the New-Jersey DiD coefficient was 2.972.97 (p=0.025p=0.025), suggesting the minimum-wage increase raised employment by about 2.97 employees per restaurant. This aligns closely with the specification originally reported in Card and Krueger (1994): their main regression results (Table 4, column (ii)) also regress change in full-time-equivalent employment on a New Jersey indicator and chain indicators, adding an indicator for company ownership, and find an increase of 2.30 employees (p=0.055p=0.055). The main differences are that Card and Krueger 1) include managers, though they exclude them as a robustness check; 2) use conventional standard errors instead of HC2; and 3) restrict their main analysis to the 357 restaurants with data on employment and starting wages in both survey waves.

Turning to our selection correction, Figure 5 shows the estimated selection multiplier λ^q,m\widehat{\lambda}_{q,m} in the left panel, and the original and corrected p-value p^q,nsel\widehat{p}^{\mathrm{sel}}_{q,n} in the right panel, both with one-sided 95% confidence bounds following Section 3.5. We find that the agent reproduces its original analysis more often when it looks favorable, reselecting it in 12.6% of tail replays but only in 7.2% of body replays. This corresponds to a selection multiplier of 1.72 with a one-sided 95% lower bound of 1.43, indicating statistically significant evidence of selection in this finding. When we calculate λ^q,m​(0.05)\widehat{\lambda}_{q,m}(0.05), i.e. the relative probability of selecting the result when it is significant at the 5% level, the multiplier increases further to 1.901.90, with a one-sided 95% lower bound of 1.55. Thus, it appears that GPT-6-Luna tends to report positive employment effects of the New Jersey minimum wage more often when it appears significant. At the same time, looking at the original and corrected pp-values in the right panel of Figure 5, we see that the original pp-value of 0.02520.0252 gets corrected upward to 0.04330.0433, so the corrected point estimate of the pp-value remains below 0.050.05, even though our conservative test based on the upper 95% confidence bound cannot reject the null anymore at 0.0520.052.

Robustness.

As we note below, a frontier AI reviewer (GPT-6.1-Sol, at high effort) judges 98.5% of GPT-6-Luna’s analyses to be methodologically sound, and 99.5% after a second model (Claude Opus 5.5, at high effort) audits its verdicts. Nonetheless, we test the robustness of these headline results to using several stronger coding models, GPT-6.1-Terra, GPT-6.1-Sol, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (all at high effort) in Table 8. The results for the two stronger GPT models are very similar, with λ^=1.79,1.98\widehat{\lambda}=1.79,1.98 and p^sel=0.051,0.053\widehat{p}^{\mathrm{sel}}=0.051,0.053, respectively. The confidence bands are slightly narrower, driven by higher reselection rates in both tail and body for both stronger GPT models. Interestingly, the estimated multipliers for Claude Sonnet 5.5 are almost exactly equal to 1, indicating Claude does not engage in selection on this application.

Looking in more detail at its logs, this appears to be driven by two factors. First, Claude explicitly refuses to pick the most compelling finding. For example, on the full dataset, Claude says explicitly, “I did not lead with the most statistically compelling result, because picking the smallest p-value from about 30 looks would overstate the evidence.” Of course, even while stating its refusal, Claude still admits that it apparently looked at 30 different results.

Second, Claude appears to recognize that the data originates from the Card and Krueger paper with much higher frequency than the GPT models, explicitly mentioning the paper in its logs 18.7% of the time, compared to none of GPT-6.1-Sol’s replays. To assess whether this is driving the lack of selection, we reran Claude on a masked version of the data, with variable names and scales, and years and proper nouns modified to hide the origin of the data. On the masked data, Claude’s estimated λ\lambda is slightly higher (1.011.01) but remains insignificantly different from 11. Importantly, this does not establish that Claude models are resistant to data-driven selection. Indeed, in Table 9, which estimates the open-ended simulation design with Claude Sonnet and Opus 5.5 (high effort), we found that Sonnet and the stronger Opus model report significant pp-values when all effects are zero 74 and 54% of the time. Thus, these results suggest that selective behavior is both model- and context-dependent, highlighting the value of our method for both detecting when coding agents engage in such behavior, and correcting for it when they do.

Agents’ choices and search.

Since the agents carry out a full empirical analysis independently in this application, we can study the decisions they make as they progress through the analysis using the agent traces. First, from the final analysis the agents commit to, as well as the code they write for it, we can observe the types of decisions the agents make for the DiD design. By executing the code the agents wrote for the analysis, we can correlate these decisions with how significant the resulting estimates are when following vs. not following the agent’s decision. In particular, we used a swarm of GPT-6.1-Sol agents to classify the analysis each replay agent committed to into the different design decisions made: what measure of employment was used as the outcome, whether the regression included chain fixed effects, and so on. Then, we re-estimated the model the agents ran under the alternative options: e.g., if the replay agent chose to use total headcount as the outcome, we recomputed their final regression on their replay data with the most-used alternative options (non-manager FTE, full-time employees, FTE including managers).

Based on that, we classified which of the choices delivered the lowest p-value and called that the “most significant” option. We find that two choices drove most of the final results’ significance: what employment measure was used, and whether chain fixed effects were included. Figure 6 shows how frequently each choice was made, split by whether it was the most significant option on the replay agent’s data or not. For each of the 4 employment options, and both of the fixed effects options, the agents chose a particular option much more frequently when it delivered the most significant results, choosing it at least 2×\times and up to 12.6×\times as frequently as the less significant options. At the same time, the employment measure used by the original analysis—Nonmanager FTE—appears to act as a default choice, being chosen 39% of the time even when it is not the most significant. This suggests that these agents did not purely make choices based on statistical significance, but also based on what they deemed to be sensible. Indeed, in support of this, in Table 7 we find that up to 99.5% of replay agents’ analyses were methodologically sound, as judged by two frontier reviewer AI models (GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, high effort). This high percentage underscores the rapid improvement in quality of coding agents’ analytic capabilities, especially compared to the lower 86% of analyses that passed AI review in Miao et al. (2026), for a different analytic task of similar difficulty.

Looking at the “p-hacking” behavior of the coding agents in more detail, Figure 8 panel (a) shows clear bunching just below p=0.05p=0.05 for the replays’ reported p-values, with panel (b) showing that this is driven mostly by specification searching relative to the original analysis, including searching over the employment outcome measure.

In addition, from the agent traces, we can observe the entire chain of “tool calls” the agent executes during its analysis — text the agent emits to instantiate an action, together with the outcome of that action. Thus, we can see what types of actions the agent executes on the data and the surrounding files, and at what stage in its analysis it does so. From the agents’ message transcript, we can also see a summary of the internal reasoning steps (“chain-of-thought”) the agent took to arrive at a decision. The results are shown in Figure 7. We classify agent actions into 8 categories: 1) set up environment; 2) inspect data; 3) write analysis script; 4) estimate or evaluate; 5) interpret or choose; 6) verify; 7) report; or 8) debug/other. Here, “estimate or evaluate” denotes instances where the agent executes an analysis (e.g. running a regression) or inspects its results, and “interpret or choose” denotes any instance where the agent compares several results from different analyses, as observed from its message transcripts or the code it executes. For the latter, the reported share of steps where this happens is a lower bound on the true frequency, as the GPT models only return summaries of their internal chain-of-thought and we expect most of the deliberation about different analyses to happen in that chain-of-thought. A more detailed description of each category is provided in the figure notes.

Looking at the results, we see that essentially all replay agents begin their analysis by inspecting the data. 85% of all steps in the first out of ten bins involve data inspection, with 94% of all replay agents inspecting the data at least once in that first bin (with the remaining 6% of agents spending the entire first bin setting up the computing environment). This supports the premise of this article that coding agents typically inspect the data before settling on an analysis, invalidating classical statistical guarantees when they do — though of course, the coding agents were partly encouraged to do so in the prompt we gave them.

The next most frequent activity agents engage in is “Estimate or evaluate”, which occurs in all bins except the first and reaches its highest frequency near the middle of the analysis chain. Note that we distinguish this activity from “write analysis script” based on whether the agent wrote the code in a separate, reproducible script or whether it executed the code directly in the terminal without writing a separate file for it. Since we instructed the agent to write reusable code for its final analysis, this allows us to distinguish between purely exploratory analysis and analysis aimed at developing the final result.

Looking at Figure 7, we see that the agents generally first engage in exploratory analysis before writing any scripts. Breaking this down for individual agents’ actions, we indeed find that 97.9% of replay agents ran an analysis before writing any external scripts, further supporting our hypothesis that these agents tend to engage in a severe form of data snooping when given a typical partly open-ended analytical task. Finally, we also observe agents starting to write their final report early on in their analysis chain, with the “Report” category showing up at the middle of the sequence and growing towards the end. This reflects agents starting to write the final report mid-analysis and then updating as they go: about 23.5% of agents edit the analysis.R script that contains their final analysis after starting to write up their report.

Agents’ self-corrections.

Finally, we noticed that agents sometimes autonomously report multiplicity corrections when they test multiple specifications. A natural question arises: could one just rely on the agents’ self-corrections to account for data-driven selection of results, without requiring a new method? A first answer to this question is theoretical: as noted by Fithian et al. (2014, Section 2.3), conditional selective inference and multiplicity correction control different error rates, and neither guarantee implies the other. A Bonferroni or Holm correction over a family ℱ\mathcal{F} of KK analyses that is fixed in advance bounds the probability of any false rejection in ℱ\mathcal{F}, and therefore covers the reported analysis unconditionally under any selection rule with values in ℱ\mathcal{F} (Berk et al., 2013). Recall (Fithian et al., 2014, e.g.) that a conditional correction is valid unconditionally as well, but not the other way around. As such, this unconditional guarantee holds only on average over the analyses the agent might report, but not for any given analysis. Under any law in which every null in ℱ\mathcal{F} holds,

∑q∈ℱPr⁡(Q=q)​λq​(u)=∑q∈ℱPr⁡(Q=q∣pq​(D)≤u)≤K,\sum_{q\in\mathcal{F}}\Pr(Q=q)\,\lambda_{q}(u)=\sum_{q\in\mathcal{F}}\Pr\!\left(Q=q\mid p_{q}(D)\leq u\right)\leq K,

so Bonferroni’s factor KK bounds the selection-weighted average of the multipliers λq\lambda_{q} that our correction estimates, and comes close to it only for an agent that reports a pp-value below uu whenever one exists, such as one that always reports the smallest pp-value, and even then only when K​uKu is small. Otherwise, a multiplicity correction overcharges analyses whose selection depends little on the data, for which λq\lambda_{q} is close to one, and can undercharge analyses that the agent reports rarely and mostly when they are significant, for which λq\lambda_{q} can exceed KK (Andrews et al., 2024; Neufeld et al., 2026, see also).

A second and more basic problem is that the agents’ own corrections do not satisfy the premise of simultaneous inference. The family to correct over must be fixed before the data are observed and contain every analysis the agent would report on any dataset (Berk et al., 2013; Kuchibhotla et al., 2022), including analyses the agent did not run on the observed data because those data led it elsewhere (Gelman and Loken, 2014). Coding agents instead count the tests they happened to run on the observed data, so that the family and its size depend on the data, and the resulting correction has no size guarantee in general. Indeed, we observe this in the corrections the replay agents propose in our experiments. For the original Card–Krueger analysis, the Sol agent explicitly counts the 26 specifications it ran and applies a Holm correction that increases the original pp-value of 0.0270.027 to 0.700.70 (the Luna agent does not supply a self-correction in its original run). The number of tests Sol counts varies widely across runs: between 6 and 194 on the subsampled datasets in Figure 9, and between 12 and 1,252 in 200 placebo runs on the full data, where we permute the treatment assignment. Moreover, 25 to 36% of the Sol replays select analyses different from the 26 that the original run accounts for. The original’s count is thus one draw from a data-dependent distribution of families, and hence the agents’ self-correction is itself data-dependent. A family large enough to be valid would have to contain every analysis the agent reports on some dataset — 129 distinct analyses across our replays — and a Bonferroni correction over 38 or more analyses already sets the original pp-value of 0.0270.027 to 11. The agent’s list is thus both too short to be valid and long enough to erase the finding. By contrast, our corrected pp-value for the Sol agent, 0.0530.053, instead charges only for how much the agent’s choice of this analysis depends on the data. Replay can do this because it fixes the selection rule, the agent with its prompt and context, rather than the family of analyses.

The third and last problem with asking agents to self-correct is practical: they do not apply their corrections consistently, either within runs of the same agent or across different agents. Table 9 classifies the frequency and types of self-corrections various agents engage in on the 100 simulations of the open-ended design from Section 4.2, where every significant finding is false. Sol, Sonnet and Opus correct nearly all of their significant leads, for a median of 312 to 378 tests counted by their own reports, while Luna corrects only 58% of them. Even when a correction is applied, it rarely reaches the headline: first, the pp-value that is actually returned as the single “compelling” finding the prompt asked for is never the corrected pp-value. As previously established, those pp-values are highly selected, with 54–98% of them falsely rejecting across the four agents. Second, in the written reports the agents return, the opening of the report gives the corrected pp-value for only 7 to 25% of significant leads, and the openings of 31–85% of the different agents’ significant reports give no concrete reason to doubt the finding. Finally, when an agent does self-correct, its list-based correction costs power, in line with the arguments in the previous paragraphs. Indeed, on 49 simulated datasets with a moderate true effect (as in our simulations’ power design) on which Sol reported the same analysis, 40 runs corrected over 18 tests and 9 applied no correction. The corrections as written keep 30 of the 49 effects, against 39 for the correction conditional on reporting that analysis (nine gains and no losses, exact paired p=0.004p=0.004; Figure 10). All nine gains have nominal pp-values between 0.003 and 0.02, above Holm’s threshold of 0.05/180.05/18, while three runs that did not correct kept findings with pp-values in the same range. On the same analysis and with nearly the same evidence, the verdict thus depended on whether the run happened to correct.

In sum, while it can certainly be useful that coding agents can exercise inherent caution against pp-hacking, agents’ self-corrections cannot be relied on to give statistical guarantees for their own selective behavior. This is the purpose of our method.

6 Conclusion

Empirical scientific research is undergoing a drastic transformation as coding agents, AI models that can interact with data and compute environments, are increasingly capable of implementing empirical analyses end-to-end. Although these improving capabilities could accelerate empirical science, they also threaten to exacerbate existing issues in applied statistics. With an army of coding agents that can implement analyses in minutes that used to take weeks, a researcher can explore a much vaster analysis space than previously possible, stretching the limits of classical statistical paradigms, which assume that the hypotheses to be tested are specified before the researcher looks at the data. At the same time, coding agents have several unique features that allow one to control the way they (are used to) select results.

This paper proposes a new method to detect and correct distortions to classical statistical guarantees for empirical research conducted by coding agents. By replaying both the agent and the statistical analysis it implements on subsampled datasets, we show how to estimate the agent’s propensity to select a given analysis when it looks statistically favorable. We can then use this propensity to restore the statistical validity of the pp-value reported by the agent. We establish the asymptotic validity and consistency of the resulting corrected pp-value, show how to construct confidence bands to account for replay uncertainty, and establish conditions under which these results hold uniformly over the class of null laws. Our simulations and applications bear out the theory and illustrate the unpredictable nature of agent-driven selection, with frontier agents refusing to engage in selection in one setting but happily pp-hacking up to 100% of their analyses in another. Our selective replay method provides the novel statistical machinery required to 1) reliably detect when agents selectively report results; and 2) restore the statistical validity of those results when they do.

Appendix A Proofs

Proof of Proposition 1.

Let μ≔ℒ⁡(Dn∣Q=q)\mu\coloneqq\mathcal{L}(D_{n}\mid Q=q) and for S⊆{1,…,n}S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\} with |S|=m|S|=m, let μS\mu_{S} denote the marginal law of DSD_{S} under μ\mu. So for every measurable set BB of size-mm datasets,

μS​(B)=μ⁡({d:dS∈B})=Pr⁡(DS∈B∣Q=q).\mu_{S}(B)=\mu\bigl(\{d:d_{S}\in B\}\bigr)=\Pr(D_{S}\in B\mid Q=q).

Defining s⁡(x)≔Pr⁡(Q=q∣Dn=x)∈[0,1]s(x)\coloneqq\Pr(Q=q\mid D_{n}=x)\in[0,1], by Bayes’ rule and conditioning on DnD_{n}, for every measurable set AA of size-nn datasets we have

μ⁡(A)=Pr⁡(Dn∈A∣Q=q)=Pr⁡(Dn∈A,Q=q)Pr⁡(Q=q)=1ρq,n​∫As⁡(x)​Pn​(𝑑x).\mu(A)=\Pr(D_{n}\in A\mid Q=q)=\frac{\Pr(D_{n}\in A,\ Q=q)}{\Pr(Q=q)}=\frac{1}{\rho_{q,n}}\int_{A}s(x)\,P^{n}(dx).

This means that μ\mu is absolutely continuous with respect to PnP^{n} with density

d​μd​Pn​(x)=s⁡(x)ρq,nPn​-almost everywhere.\frac{d\mu}{dP^{n}}(x)=\frac{s(x)}{\rho_{q,n}}\qquad P^{n}\text{-almost everywhere}.

Using this density and the fact that s⁡(x)≤1s(x)\leq 1, we have

KL(μ∥Pn)=∫log(d​μd​Pn(x))μ(dx)=∫logs(x)μ(dx)+log1ρq,n≤log1ρq,n.\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|P^{n})=\int\log\!\left(\frac{d\mu}{dP^{n}}(x)\right)\,\mu(dx)=\int\log s(x)\,\mu(dx)+\log\frac{1}{\rho_{q,n}}\leq\log\frac{1}{\rho_{q,n}}.

This bounds the selection-induced divergence of the full dataset. We next use Han’s inequality to control the average divergence of its size-mm coordinate marginals in terms of this full-dataset divergence. In fact, since PnP^{n} is a product measure, Han’s inequality for relative entropy Han, 1978; Boucheron et al., 2013, Theorem 4.9 gives, for every k≤nk\leq n and every TT with |T|=k|T|=k, k−1∑i∈TKL(μT∖{i}∥Pk−1)≤k−1kKL(μT∥Pk)k^{-1}\sum_{i\in T}\mathrm{KL}(\mu_{T\setminus\{i\}}\|P^{k-1})\leq\frac{k-1}{k}\mathrm{KL}(\mu_{T}\|P^{k}). Averaging over TT and iterating from k=nk=n down to k=m+1k=m+1 yields

(nm)−1∑|S|=mKL(μS∥Pm)≤mnKL(μ∥Pn).\binom{n}{m}^{-1}\sum_{|S|=m}\mathrm{KL}\big(\mu_{S}\,\|\,P^{m}\big)\leq\frac{m}{n}\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\mu\,\|\,P^{n}\big).

Because SmS_{m} is independent of (Dn,Ξ)(D_{n},\Xi), and hence of QQ, each subset is drawn with probability (nm)−1\binom{n}{m}^{-1} regardless of whether qq is selected, so ℒ⁡(DSm∣Q=q)=(nm)−1​∑|S|=mμS\mathcal{L}(D_{S_{m}}\mid Q=q)=\binom{n}{m}^{-1}\sum_{|S|=m}\mu_{S}. Hence

KL(ℒ(DSm∣Q=q)∥Pm)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal{L}(D_{S_{m}}\mid Q=q)\,\|\,P^{m}\big) ≤(nm)−1∑|S|=mKL(μS∥Pm)\displaystyle\leq\binom{n}{m}^{-1}\sum_{|S|=m}\mathrm{KL}\big(\mu_{S}\,\|\,P^{m}\big) (convexity of relative entropy)
≤mnKL(μ∥Pn)\displaystyle\leq\frac{m}{n}\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\mu\,\|\,P^{n}\big) (Han’s inequality)
≤mn​log⁡1ρq,n,\displaystyle\leq\frac{m}{n}\log\frac{1}{\rho_{q,n}},

and Pinsker’s inequality Pinsker, 1964; Boucheron et al., 2013, Theorem 4.19 gives the result. ∎

Appendix B Proofs for statistical results in Section 3

Proof of Proposition 2.

Conditional on Qn=qQ_{n}=q, Hq,nH_{q,n} is the cdf of Uq,nU_{q,n}. For any cdf HH, let X∼HX\sim H and let V∼Unif⁡(0,1)V\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1) be independent of XX. The randomized probability integral transform

T=H⁡(X−)+V⁡[H⁡(X)−H⁡(X−)],T=H(X^{-})+V\bigl[H(X)-H(X^{-})\bigr],

where H⁡(x−)=limy↑xH⁡(y)H(x^{-})=\lim_{y\uparrow x}H(y), is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1] (Rüschendorf, 2009, Prop. 2.1). Writing

ΔH≔supx[H⁡(x)−H⁡(x−)]\Delta_{H}\coloneqq\sup_{x}\bigl[H(x)-H(x^{-})\bigr]

for the largest jump of HH, we have 0≤H⁡(X)−T=(1−V)​[H⁡(X)−H⁡(X−)]≤ΔH.0\leq H(X)-T=(1-V)\bigl[H(X)-H(X^{-})\bigr]\leq\Delta_{H}. In our setting, every such jump is bounded by

PrP⁡(Uq,n=u∣Qn=q)≤Fq,n​(u)−Fq,n​(u−)ρq,n≤2ρq,n​supv∈[0,1]|Fq,n​(v)−v|⟶0,\Pr_{P}(U_{q,n}=u\mid Q_{n}=q)\leq\frac{F_{q,n}(u)-F_{q,n}(u^{-})}{\rho_{q,n}}\leq\frac{2}{\rho_{q,n}}\sup_{v\in[0,1]}\left|F_{q,n}(v)-v\right|\longrightarrow 0,

by Assumptions 3 and 5. As a result, for Vq,n=Hq,n​(Uq,n)V_{q,n}=H_{q,n}(U_{q,n}),

0≤α−PrP⁡(Vq,n≤α∣Qn=q)→0.0\leq\alpha-\Pr_{P}(V_{q,n}\leq\alpha\mid Q_{n}=q)\to 0. (20)

∎

Lemma 2 (Subsampling cdf bound).

Let TT be any measurable statistic of a dataset of size mm which may depend on the ordering of its observations and on auxiliary randomness Ξ\Xi. Let GG be its cdf under PmP^{m} and GnSG_{n}^{S} its conditional cdf under a uniformly drawn and randomly ordered size-mm subset of DnD_{n}, that is,

GnS​(t):=Pr⁡(T⁡(DSm,Ξ′)≤t∣Dn).G_{n}^{S}(t):=\Pr\left(T(D_{S_{m}},\Xi^{\prime})\leq t\mid D_{n}\right).

Under Assumption 1, with K=⌊n/m⌋K=\lfloor n/m\rfloor,

PrP⁡(‖GnS−G‖∞>x)≤3​e−K​x2.\Pr_{P}\bigl(\|G_{n}^{S}-G\|_{\infty}>x\bigr)\leq 3e^{-Kx^{2}}.

Conditional on Qn=qQ_{n}=q, this probability is at most 3​e−K​x2/ρq,n3e^{-Kx^{2}}/\rho_{q,n}.

Proof.

Randomly partition the nn observations into KK disjoint blocks of size mm. Let G^K\widehat{G}_{K} be the empirical cdf of TT on these blocks, using the independence of Ξ\Xi across blocks. Unconditionally, the block statistics are i.i.d. with cdf GG. As a result, the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz–Massart inequality (Dvoretzky et al., 1956; Massart, 1990) gives

PrP⁡(‖G^K−G‖∞>x)≤2​e−2​K​x2.\Pr_{P}\bigl(\|\widehat{G}_{K}-G\|_{\infty}>x\bigr)\leq 2e^{-2Kx^{2}}.

Since each block is marginally a uniformly drawn subset of size mm, GnS=𝔼⁡(G^K∣Dn)G_{n}^{S}=\mathbb{E}(\widehat{G}_{K}\mid D_{n}), and we have

𝔼​exp⁡{K​‖GnS−G‖∞2}\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\exp\{K\|G_{n}^{S}-G\|_{\infty}^{2}\} ≤𝔼​exp⁡{K​‖G^K−G‖∞2}\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\exp\{K\|\widehat{G}_{K}-G\|_{\infty}^{2}\}
=1+∫0∞et​Pr⁡(K​‖G^K−G‖∞2>t)​𝑑t\displaystyle=1+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{t}\Pr\!\left(K\|\widehat{G}_{K}-G\|_{\infty}^{2}>t\right)\,dt
≤1+2​∫0∞e−t​dt=3,\displaystyle\leq 1+2\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}\,dt=3,

by Jensen’s inequality, the layer-cake representation, and the tail bound above, respectively. Then, Markov’s inequality gives the first claim. The second claim follows by noting that PrP⁡(E∣Qn=q)≤PrP⁡(E)/ρq,n\Pr_{P}(E\mid Q_{n}=q)\leq\Pr_{P}(E)/\rho_{q,n} for any event EE. ∎

Lemma 3 (Stability of selected-rank distributions).

Under Assumptions 3, 4(a), and 5, for every ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2),

supu∈[ε,1−ε][Hq,n​(u)−Hq,mn​(u)]+⟶0.\sup_{u\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]}[H_{q,n}(u)-H_{q,m_{n}}(u)]_{+}\longrightarrow 0.

If Assumption 4(b) holds, the conclusion here also holds with an absolute value.

Proof.

Write κq,k=supu|Fq,k​(u)−u|\kappa_{q,k}=\sup_{u}|F_{q,k}(u)-u|, which tends to zero for both k=n,mnk=n,m_{n}. For any 0≤a<b≤10\leq a<b\leq 1 and either sample size k=n,mnk=n,m_{n},

Hq,k​(b)−Hq,k​(a)≤Fq,k​(b)−Fq,k​(a)ρq,k≤b−a+2​κq,kρ⋆.H_{q,k}(b)-H_{q,k}(a)\leq\frac{F_{q,k}(b)-F_{q,k}(a)}{\rho_{q,k}}\leq\frac{b-a+2\kappa_{q,k}}{\rho_{\star}}.

At each fixed u>0u>0, the identity Hq,k​(u)=Fq,k​(u)​λq,k​(u)H_{q,k}(u)=F_{q,k}(u)\lambda_{q,k}(u) and Assumptions 3 and 4 give

[Hq,n​(u)−Hq,mn​(u)]+≤[λq,n​(u)−λq,mn​(u)]++κq,n+κq,mnρ⋆⟶0.[H_{q,n}(u)-H_{q,m_{n}}(u)]_{+}\leq[\lambda_{q,n}(u)-\lambda_{q,m_{n}}(u)]_{+}+\frac{\kappa_{q,n}+\kappa_{q,m_{n}}}{\rho_{\star}}\longrightarrow 0.

Then, fix a finite grid ε=t0<⋯<tL=1−ε\varepsilon=t_{0}<\cdots<t_{L}=1-\varepsilon with mesh at most hh. By monotonicity of the cdfs, for any u∈[tj,tj+1]u\in[t_{j},t_{j+1}],

Hq,n​(u)−Hq,mn​(u)\displaystyle H_{q,n}(u)-H_{q,m_{n}}(u) ≤Hq,n​(tj+1)−Hq,mn​(tj)\displaystyle\leq H_{q,n}(t_{j+1})-H_{q,m_{n}}(t_{j}) (21)
≤Hq,n​(tj+1)−Hq,mn​(tj+1)+h+2​κq,mnρ⋆,\displaystyle\leq H_{q,n}(t_{j+1})-H_{q,m_{n}}(t_{j+1})+\frac{h+2\kappa_{q,m_{n}}}{\rho_{\star}},

where the second inequality follows from the first bound above. As a result,

where the maximum vanishes by the pointwise convergence shown above since we work on a finite grid, and κq,mn→0\kappa_{q,m_{n}}\to 0 by Assumption 3. Since h>0h>0 is arbitrary, the result follows. The case with an absolute value also follows by the same argument with nn and mnm_{n} interchanged. ∎

Proof of Corollary 1.

Throughout, we write m=mnm=m_{n}, un=Uq,nu_{n}=U_{q,n}, and VnP=Hq,nP​(un)V_{n}^{P}=H^{P}_{q,n}(u_{n}). All suprema over PP below are taken over the set of null distributions 𝔓0,q\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}. For ε∈(0,1/2)\varepsilon\in(0,1/2), we define

Iε=[ε,1−ε],En,ε={un∈Iε}.I_{\varepsilon}=[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon],\quad E_{n,\varepsilon}=\{u_{n}\in I_{\varepsilon}\}.

We first make the estimation argument in the proof of Theorem 1 uniform over PP. The subsampling bounds used there are distribution-free. Conditioning on Qn=qQ_{n}=q increases an unconditional probability bound by at most a factor 1/ρ⋆1/\rho_{\star}. Since ⌊n/mn⌋→∞\lfloor n/m_{n}\rfloor\to\infty, the corresponding approximation errors vanish uniformly in conditional probability over 𝔓0,q\mathfrak{P}_{0,q}.

For adaptive replay counts, the union bound over replay prefixes in the same proof bounds the probability that either replay frequency is unavailable or differs from its stratum selection probability bs,nb_{s,n} under the subsampling law by more than δ>0\delta>0, uniformly over PP, by

supPPrP⁡(mins∈{0,1}⁡Bs,n<M|Qn=q)+4​e−2​M​δ21−e−2​δ2.\sup_{P}\Pr_{P}\!\left(\min_{s\in\{0,1\}}B_{s,n}<M\,\middle|\,Q_{n}=q\right)+\frac{4e^{-2M\delta^{2}}}{1-e^{-2\delta^{2}}}.

Letting n→∞n\to\infty and then M→∞M\to\infty, this bound vanishes under Assumption 9.

On En,εE_{n,\varepsilon}, the uniform calibration bounds both population stratum probabilities below by ε−κn\varepsilon-\kappa_{n}. The population correction denominator is at least ρ⋆−κn\rho_{\star}-\kappa_{n}, by the denominator calculation in the proof of Theorem 1. The preceding uniform consistency bounds ensure that the corresponding subsampling denominators are also bounded away from zero with probability tending uniformly to one on this event. Thus, the ratio and calibration arguments in that proof give, for every δ>0\delta>0,

supPPrP(En,ε∩{|p^q,nsel−Hq,mP(un)|>δ}|Qn=q)→0.\sup_{P}\Pr_{P}\!\left(E_{n,\varepsilon}\cap\left\{\left|\widehat{p}^{\mathrm{sel}}_{q,n}-H^{P}_{q,m}(u_{n})\right|>\delta\right\}\,\middle|\,Q_{n}=q\right)\to 0.

Next, we make the selected-cdf stability argument uniform. The increment bound in Lemma 3 becomes

Hq,kP​(b)−Hq,kP​(a)≤b−a+2​κnρ⋆,k∈{n,m},0≤a<b≤1.H^{P}_{q,k}(b)-H^{P}_{q,k}(a)\leq\frac{b-a+2\kappa_{n}}{\rho_{\star}},\quad k\in\{n,m\},\quad 0\leq a<b\leq 1.

Thus, for a fixed finite grid 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h} that covers IεI_{\varepsilon} with a mesh size of at most hh, the finite-grid argument of that lemma gives

supPsupu∈Iε[Hq,nP​(u)−Hq,mP​(u)]+≤max⁡supPt∈𝒯h⁡[λq,nP​(t)−λq,mP​(t)]++h+4​κnρ⋆.\sup_{P}\sup_{u\in I_{\varepsilon}}[H^{P}_{q,n}(u)-H^{P}_{q,m}(u)]_{+}\leq\max_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{h}}\sup_{P}[\lambda^{P}_{q,n}(t)-\lambda^{P}_{q,m}(t)]_{+}+\frac{h+4\kappa_{n}}{\rho_{\star}}.

The maximum tends to zero by Assumption 8(a), since the grid is finite and independent of PP. Letting n→∞n\to\infty and then h↓0h\downarrow 0 proves uniform one-sided cdf stability on IεI_{\varepsilon}. Under Assumption 8(b), the same argument gives the corresponding absolute-value bound.

Combining estimation and stability on En,εE_{n,\varepsilon}, and using the endpoint bound from the proof of Theorem 1,

supPPrP⁡(En,εc∣Qn=q)≤2​ε+2​κnρ⋆,\sup_{P}\Pr_{P}(E_{n,\varepsilon}^{c}\mid Q_{n}=q)\leq\frac{2\varepsilon+2\kappa_{n}}{\rho_{\star}},

we obtain, by first letting n→∞n\to\infty and then ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0, that for every η>0\eta>0,

rn​(η):=supPPrP⁡(VnP−p^q,nsel>η|Qn=q)→0.r_{n}(\eta):=\sup_{P}\Pr_{P}\!\left(V_{n}^{P}-\widehat{p}^{\mathrm{sel}}_{q,n}>\eta\,\middle|\,Q_{n}=q\right)\to 0.

Under two-sided stability, the same conclusion holds for rnabs​(η)r_{n}^{\mathrm{abs}}(\eta), defined by replacing the discrepancy inside this probability with its absolute value.

Finally, the oracle super-uniformity from Proposition 2 gives

Any shifted thresholds outside [0,1][0,1] are handled by the trivial probability bounds zero and one. Letting n→∞n\to\infty and then η↓0\eta\downarrow 0 proves both conclusions. ∎

Proof of Proposition 3.

+PrP0⁡(|Vn0−α|≤η∣Qn=q).\displaystyle+\Pr_{P_{0}}\left(|V_{n}^{0}-\alpha|\leq\eta\mid Q_{n}=q\right).

The first term converges to zero by the two-sided conclusion of Theorem 1. By Proposition 2, the limsup of the second term is at most 2​η2\eta. Letting η↓0\eta\downarrow 0 establishes that the disagreement probability vanishes under P0P_{0}, conditional on Qn=qQ_{n}=q.

Let

En={𝟏{p^q,nsel≤α}≠𝟏{Vn0≤α},Qn=q}.E_{n}=\left\{\mathbf{1}\{\widehat{p}_{q,n}^{\mathrm{sel}}\leq\alpha\}\neq\mathbf{1}\{V_{n}^{0}\leq\alpha\},\ Q_{n}=q\right\}.

where the probability is taken over the original agent and replay randomizations. Since these randomizations have the same conditional law given DnD_{n} under P0P_{0} and PnP_{n}, the function fnf_{n} is common to both experiments.

By the preceding argument,

𝔼P0n​[fn​(Dn)]=PrP0⁡(En)⟶0,\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}^{n}}[f_{n}(D_{n})]=\Pr_{P_{0}}(E_{n})\longrightarrow 0,

where P0nP_{0}^{n} is the sampling distribution of DnD_{n} under the null law P0P_{0}. Thus, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, by Markov’s inequality,

P0n​(fn​(Dn)>ε)⟶0,P_{0}^{n}(f_{n}(D_{n})>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow 0,

and by contiguity,

Pnn​(fn​(Dn)>ε)⟶0.P_{n}^{n}(f_{n}(D_{n})>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow 0.

PrPn⁡(En∣Qn=q)=PrPn⁡(En)PrPn⁡(Qn=q)⟶0,\Pr_{P_{n}}(E_{n}\mid Q_{n}=q)=\frac{\Pr_{P_{n}}(E_{n})}{\Pr_{P_{n}}(Q_{n}=q)}\longrightarrow 0,

Appendix C Additional results

C.1 Definitions

This section defines the terms from the AI literature that the paper uses and relates them to the objects of Section 2.1. The definitions are meant to give a concise understanding of the concepts involved and are by no means exhaustive. See Korinek (2025) for an introduction to AI agents for economic research.

Large language model.

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network, typically a transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), trained on large amounts of text to predict the next token (a word or word fragment) given the preceding ones (Brown et al., 2020). It generates text by drawing a token from this predicted distribution of tokens, appending it to its input, and repeating. The input is called the context, and the part of the context that contains the user’s instructions is called the prompt. Input and output are text (character strings) in a broad sense that includes prose, code, and shell commands. Many current models first generate intermediate reasoning tokens that are fed back into the model with the aim of improving the accuracy of the final answer, called a chain of thought (Wei et al., 2022). The user can specify how much of this reasoning the models are required to perform (the “reasoning effort”; OpenAI, 2026). Two properties of these models are important for this paper: first, because tokens are drawn at random, the same context (input) can produce different outputs; second, the model’s parameters do not change during use, so the model does not retain any memory from one conversation to the next (not counting renewed ingestion of external inputs as “memory”).

Agent.

In the classical definition in the field of AI, an agent is anything that can perceive its environment and intervene in it (Russell and Norvig, 2021, Chapter 2). An LLM becomes an agent through tool calling: the model emits text in a prescribed format that names an action (a “tool”, e.g. running a shell command) and its arguments, a computer program then executes the prescribed action in the embedded computing environment and appends the result to the context, and the expanded context is fed back to the model so that it receives environmental feedback from its action (Yao et al., 2023). Current usage of the term “agent” largely reserves it for systems in which the model itself decides which actions to take and in what order, as opposed to workflows in which a programmer fixes the sequence of model calls in advance, which are encompassed by the broader classical definition (Anthropic, 2024). A common short definition is that an LLM agent “runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal” (Willison, 2025).

Harness.

A program that executes an agentic loop is called a harness. In one common formulation, the harness denotes every part of an agentic system other than the model itself (Trivedy, 2026). It assembles the context, including a system prompt with standing instructions and descriptions of the available tools, sends it to the model, and executes the tool calls that the model requests, subject to the permissions granted by the user. The model is usually hosted by a provider on a server in a data center and queried through an API over the internet, while the harness runs in a separate compute environment. Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) and the Codex CLI, used in this paper, each combine a harness with a command-line interface.

Coding agent.

A coding agent is an LLM agent whose available tools let it read and write files and execute programs on a computer (Lucas and Open Interpreter Contributors, 2023; Yang et al., 2024). Statistical software can be run programmatically, usually through the command line, so such an agent can load a dataset, write code to estimate a statistical model, execute that code, read the output, and revise its code in response. We call the folder that the agent can read and modify its workspace, one execution of the loop from the initial prompt to the agent’s final answer a run or session, and the record of all messages, tool calls, and results emitted by a coding agent and its program executions in a run its trace or log.

Relation to the formal setup.

In the notation of Section 2.1, 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} comprises the base model, the harness, the tools, and their settings, such as the reasoning effort; rr collects the instructions (the prompt) and the files other than the data that are available to the agent at the start of a run; and Ξ\Xi collects intrinsic model randomness (due to the token draws and other nondeterminism in LLM inference) and any additional randomness in the tool results. Because the model does not retain any context across runs, a new run that starts from the same rr in a fresh copy of the workspace, with the model and harness held fixed, applies the same mapping with a fresh draw of Ξ\Xi, which is the sense in which a coding agent can be reset and replayed. Finally, some harnesses provide a way for the model to store notes that persist across runs. Since these are stored outside the model and enter a run by being reinjected into the model’s context, holding them fixed is part of holding rr fixed.

C.3 Ideological bias and immigration

This Appendix section describes our replication of the results in Miao et al. (2026) in some more detail and reports the corresponding results on the faulty data file included in their replication package.

Replication.

The design involves rerunning the coding agents on the full datasets, as opposed to on subsamples as in our method, and changing the agents’ prompts to induce diverse perspectives in their analysis. Any given analysis reported by one single agent is then tested against the resulting reference distribution of analyses for how extreme it is, similar to a two-sided p-value. As discussed in Section 2.3, the authors call this an “m-value”, and suggest that it captures “the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one”. Table 2 reports the results, for the AI model used by the authors (Claude Sonnet 4.6, through the Claude Agent SDK) as well as a more recent version of the same model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) and GPT-6-Luna (through the Codex CLI). As in the original paper, we ran 20 pro- and 20 anti-immigration agents on the same data, and subjected the agents’ outputs to a three-stage methodological review to filter out incorrect analyses. Any remaining small differences from the authors’ results are likely due to LLM stochasticity and the fact that we used a more recent model as the methodology judge (GPT-6.1-Sol instead of GPT-5.4).

Design.

We refer to Miao et al. (2026) and the accompanying replication package for the details on their design, and just highlight some more details on how we deviated from it here. The Claude runs use the harness settings of Miao et al. (2026) in the Claude Agent SDK, which use the default high effort setting. Since the SDK runs Claude Code CLI under the hood, for the GPT-6-Luna runs, we use the analogous Codex CLI at high reasoning effort. We pass the persona prompts as the system prompt in both harnesses, replacing the default system prompt. Following the paper, each final result produced by an agent undergoes an “inference repair” where a separate, independent reviewer agent (same model as the original) reviews and fixes any methodological errors it can find in the code. Finally, each analysis undergoes a methodological review of a structured summary of the repaired specification, run three times with the review prompt provided in the replication package. A result is kept if at least two of the three verdicts pass it, and its zz-statistic is recovered from the repaired two-sided pp-value. As noted above, summary and review use GPT-6.1-Sol whereas theirs use GPT-5.4. Since the authors did not publish their summary agent’s prompt, we construct it from their example summaries.

Data.

We noticed several data mismatches in the file distributed by Miao et al. (2026), with respondents being assigned the wrong country and outcome columns holding survey questions, likely due to a faulty data merge. We rebuilt the file ourselves from the ISSP archive releases and the replication package of Breznau et al. (2022) and use the corrected file for our analyses. Our results with Claude Sonnet 4.6 are close to the authors’ on both files and, if anything, closer on the corrected file (Tables 2 and 4: a gap in mean zz of −4.5-4.5, against −3.8-3.8 on their file and −4.2-4.2 in their paper), so we suspect the faulty merge arose in the replication package rather than in the analysis behind the paper. Table 3 lists all the variables in the data that were given to the agent and hence available to choose for its analysis. For full transparency, Table 4 reports our replication results on the faulty data file, which still gives highly similar results.

Reference distribution for the m-value.

The m-value of the application’s original uses 60 full-data GPT-6-Luna sessions with the original’s harness and data: 20 with the original request, 20 with the team described as pushing for lower immigration to protect a strong safety net, and 20 with a nonpartisan team. Their logs hold 811 estimated analyses, nearly all with standard errors clustered by country. The m-value pools them with equal weight, as in the calculator of Miao et al. (2026); weighting sessions equally gives 0.25.

C.3.1 Known selection rules on a fixed menu

As a complement to the fixed simulation design in Section 4.2, we also considered a design for the immigration application where the agents were told to implement a known selection rule on the data. This allows us to compare our estimated pp-values to the oracle pp-values, which are known exactly because we fixed the selection rule. We gave GPT-6-Luna (high effort) a menu of 108 OLS regressions of country-level support for the six welfare-related outcomes in the ISSP data on the foreign-born share, varying the item, the source of the immigrant-stock measure, the countries covered and the controls, with HC3 standard errors. An anti- and a pro-immigration analyst both gave the agent one of three instructions: report a specification named in advance whatever its result (“fixed model”); report the specification with the most negative/positive tt-statistic (“frontier”); or report the named specification if it is negative/positive and significant, and otherwise report the most negative/positive alternative (“client pressure”).

The named specification for the anti-immigration analyst regresses support for government responsibility for the unemployed on a measure of the share of immigrants in the country without controls. It is the most negative specification on the full dataset (p=0.026p=0.026), so all three workflows report it as the “original” analysis, differing only in what they report on the subsampled datasets. Then, we replayed each workflow on 100-200 subsampled datasets per stratum (tail vs. body) and computed the oracle corrected pp-value by applying the mechanical selection rules to an enlarged bank of 20,00020{,}000 subsampled datasets. Every replay agent followed the rule it was assigned exactly.

Table 5 shows that the corrected pp-values computed from the agent replays are very close to their oracle counterparts. As expected, the rule that instructed the agent to always pick the same analysis has an estimated multiplier of exactly 11, while for the anti-immigration analyst, the other rules estimate λ\lambdas larger than 11, and more strongly so for the most selective rule, which discards the original analysis whenever it is not significant.

Interestingly, we find no evidence of strong selection under these rules for the pro-immigration analyst, which appears to be driven by the fact that it fails to find significant results in its original analysis to begin with (p=0.755p=0.755 and 0.9190.919).

In the Card–Krueger application, the reported verdicts come from a separate reviewing agent.
